en: Nor is it the case that *satpratipakṣatā* (counter-balanced opposition) is not accepted for a reason characterized by pervasion in the form of co-occurrence with the pervader (*vyāpaka-sāmānādhikaraṇya*); rather, *satpratipakṣatā* belongs only to a subject (*pakṣa*) that does not reside in what is pervaded (*vahnimad-avṛtti-mat*), otherwise...

It should not be argued that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as a mountain possessing water at a time when there is the absence of fire pervading water; for even so, the non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the contradiction—defined as a reason being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum—remains unaddressed, since that too is indeed the object of the obstructive cognition occurring at the time of the cognition of the reason’s presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Nor is it the case that...

Since having that [the subject] as its object (*tadviṣayakatva*) occurs in a locus other than the state of being an inhibitor (*pratibandhakatā*), how could it be subsumed under the general definition? This is because, if one accepts that only such a reason qualified by subsisting in the subject (*pakṣavṛttitva*) constitutes a contradiction (*virodha*), then in cases such as "The mountain possesses fire because of water," and so forth...

It should not be argued that there is no possibility of water and the like being contradictory [to the probandum] because they are the counter-correlates of absences that pervade the locus of the probandum (the *pakṣa*), since they do not reside in the *pakṣa* itself. For we accept that the final meaning of the stated definition is as follows: "A defect (*doṣa*) is that which is delimited by a specific form (*tad-rūpa*) such that, in every certainty (*niścaya*) having that form as its object, there is an absence of both (1) non-obstructiveness to inference and (2) contemporaneity with the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). If this is said, we reply: No.
In that context, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*),

such a certainty (*niścaya*) must be qualified by the condition of being devoid of any objective content (*viṣayatā*) delimited by something that is not a delimitor (*anavacchedaka*) of the obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatā*) of the inference under consideration (*prakṛtānumiti*). And [this applies to] a certainty whose object is the aforementioned qualified [entity].

Since [the cognition] possesses a subjectivity delimited by such a state of being the locus (*ādheyatā*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) therein. This is because even the certainty "the lake possesses the absence of fire" possesses an undelimited primary objecthood (*niravacchinna-viśeṣyatā*) characterized by a modehood (*prakāratā*) of such a "lake-ness. Thus it was stated.
"Delimited by something. Although this being the case,

there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a single part, because even a certainty (*niścaya*) whose object is a single part— such as "the lake possesses the absence of fire"— is of that nature, nevertheless, regarding certainty...

Even if one were to include the condition of being devoid of a subjectivity that does not constitute the subjectivity delimited by a specific form (*yadrūpāvacchinnaviṣayitvāghaṭakaviṣayitāśūnyatva*), that [definition] must also be rejected,

because such a certainty (*niścaya*) whose object is only a single part is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). Rather, there must be the status of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of a difference co-extensive with such a subjectivity.

It should be understood that this means "not being a constituent part of that. And thus, even the aforementioned cumbersome qualification need not be provided at all in order to exclude the cognition "the possessor of genus (jāti) possesses the absence of fire," precisely because the objective content (*viṣayatā*) of such a cognition is not a determinant of the state of being an obstructer (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka*).

Precisely because that [undesired consequence] can be excluded in this way, there is no harm even if both "the absence of another" (*anya-bhāva*) and "lake-ness" (*hradatva*) are included by the term *yadrūpa* (of whatever form), according to the author's natural intention in writing; for the aforementioned non-obstructive cognitions are excluded by this very qualification.

Thus, in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to such fallacies as "being cognizable" (*prameyatva*) when qualified [by another property], the inclusion of the condition "not being constituted by another such qualified entity" (*tādṛśaviśiṣṭāntarāghaṭitatva*) need not even be adopted;
this results in great parsimony (*lāghava*), since it achieves an excellence of simplicity. In fact...

To avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to what has been stated as qualified, one must adopt as a qualification the property of being the object of a cognition that is devoid of any objective content (*viṣayatā*) delimited by some [property] that is not, in its own right, a delimitor of the nature of the obstructive capacity (*pratibandhakatā*).

The author’s intention in the portion of the text beginning with "the qualificand-element consisting of the fact that the objectivity delimited by a certain form resides in a certainty qualified by the absence of non-pervasive objectivity, etc. is precisely to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as a single part [of a locus]. This is the general direction. Some, however, maintain that in order to avoid over-extension in the aforementioned qualified [pseudo-reason], the property of being a certainty whose objectivity is a certain qualified entity, which is further qualified by a certainty whose objectivity is another certain qualified entity, must reside in no more than the obstructiveness to inference (*anumitipratibandhakatā*).

Such a qualified [object] should be specified as being the object of a cognition that is devoid of both such qualified objective contents (*viṣayitā*), provided that the non-restriction of the obstructive power (*pratibandhakatā*) by the qualification of knowledge (*jñāna-vaiśiṣṭya*) does not serve as the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for those two such qualified objective contents. Furthermore, within the objective content of each of the two qualified [objects], the qualification of the non-restriction of the obstructive power by the qualification of knowledge must be applied.

They say that by adding the qualification "not being the delimitor of a non-overlapping counter-correlativity of the state of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatā) which is not delimited by the state of being qualified by cognition" to the state of having as its object two distinct [factors], there is no risk of the definition being impossible (asaṃbhava) in the case of a mountain possessing the absence of fire (vahnimad-bheda), even though the state of being a certainty whose object is a mountain possessing the absence of fire— qualified by a certainty whose object is the absence of fire— is a property that occurs in a domain no larger than the state of being an obstructor to inference. [This refers to the phrase] "qualified by the nature of being an inconstancy (vyabhicāra), etc."

Because of such conventional usage as "smoke is deviant with respect to fire" and "there is sublation of the probandum in the subject," it is well-established that "residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" is the meaning of "deviance," and "the absence of the probandum itself" is the meaning of "sublation. Therefore, in the present context, "residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" alone constitutes the meaning of "deviance."
By the phrase "because it does not deviate from awakening" (*bodhyāvyabhicārāt*), the sublation (*bādha*) consisting of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is included.
[The phrase] "of that very [property] which has such a qualified locus as its cause" means that, and thus,
for the cognition "substance-ness residing in that which possesses the absence of fire."

The point is that since [the cognition of smoke as qualified by such substanceness] does not act as an obstacle to the inference caused by that [smoke], even though smoke is qualified by such substanceness, there is no undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the conventional usage "smoke is defective.
Now, regarding the phrase "caused by that": it is not the case that being caused by that means occurring after the consideration (parāmarśa) of that [reason].

Thus, it must be said that following the consideration of both [reasons], where there is a cognition of deviation in one reason, the inference [arising] from that [second reason] is subject to deviation because it is caused by both;
this is so by virtue of the relation of "immediately preceding."

Because, in the present context, the nature of being caused by that [reason] consists precisely in being other than what is qualified by the cognition of deviation regarding that reason as its property-bearer (*dharmika*). The phrase "the delimitor of the obstructiveness to the inference under consideration" implies "by way of being its object," and so forth. Thus, [the definition is]: being such that the state of having a particular qualified thing as its object does not extend beyond the obstructiveness to inference, while at the same time not being composed of another such qualified thing.

The ultimate meaning is that the nature of the qualified object is such that the defect is of that same kind. Since "non-composition" (aghaṭitatva) consists in being the object of a cognition that does not have that [defect] as its object, there would be the fallacy of impossibility (asaṃbhava), because a thing cannot be the object of a cognition that has itself as its object.

This is the intermediate term (*antarapada*). And that [term] does not have a meaning distinct from itself, because it would be impossible to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) since fallacy (*vyabhicāra*), for instance, is non-different from "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*) as qualified by fallacy;
rather, its meaning is "being the object of a cognition that does not have itself as its object. Although...

In cases such as "knowability (prameyatva) [is absent] because it does not reside in what is non-resident in knowability," there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) regarding the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra), which consists of residing in that which resides in what lacks the absence of non-residence; for that [deviation] is constituted by the sublation (bādha) consisting of residing in what is resident in knowability. Therefore, in the definition of the nature of the obstructive factor (pratibandhakatā), the condition of "not being delimited by the fact of having another qualified entity as its object" must be applied specifically to that [obstructive factor].

It should be noted that there is no lack of the aforementioned pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the status of being a subverter (bādha), because the objective content (viṣayatā) of a subverter lacks the property of being a pervader of the counter-entailingness (pratibandhakatā) of the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti). Some, however, maintain that by incorporating the condition of "not being composed of another qualified entity similar to itself," the aforementioned defect does not arise; [this applies] to the subverter (bādha).

They say that there is no fault because, by way of the nature that divides fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), there is an absence of being of the same class as deviation (*vyabhicāra*). That is not satisfying. Similarity must be intended precisely by way of the nature that divides fallacious reasons, which is not constituted by the non-inclusion of another qualified entity; otherwise—

Since there is no definition that serves as a differentiator for fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) such as "knowability qualified by deviation" (*vyabhicāraviśiṣṭameyatva*), it is impossible to refer to it by its own term; therefore, [the definition must consist in] being other than that which is composed of another qualified entity, namely, knowability qualified by deviation and so forth.

Because that [definition] would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) since it exists there; and thus it should be noted that sublation (*bādha*) is also of the same genus as deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the nature of sublation—which is not constituted by being unconstituted by another qualified entity—exists even in the case of deviation. Furthermore, if the word "self" (*sva*) refers only to the correlate (*anuyogi*), then that which is of the same genus as the self is another qualified entity.

The definition is simply "being the object of a cognition that does not have that [the thing defined] as its object. The qualifying portion (the viśeṣya) need not be included at all; for, since things such as an indifferent jar are not over-extended [into the definition], this is because their own similar class (*sajātīya*) is simply unestablished. Thus, even similarity (*sājātya*) [is unnecessary].
It must be intended precisely as the form that distinguishes the complete fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

For, in cases such as "errancy" (*vyabhicāra*) qualified by "knowability" (*meyatva*), since the state of being pure errancy also exists, it is possible for that [qualified] errancy to belong to the same class as that [pure errancy]. And thus, regarding "knowability" qualified by errancy...
If it is argued that there is no over-extension precisely because [the property] is not established as being of the same class as itself,
then one should note that, according to this view, there is no fault other than the contradiction with the root [text]. And in this context,
the fault is the deviation qualified by cognisability (*prameyatva*).

This effort should be understood as being for the purpose of avoiding such usage, because of the absence of [the required] conventional designation (*vyavahāra*). Although even if "not being composed of another qualified entity" (*viśiṣṭāntarāghaṭitatva*) were included, such usage would still be difficult to prevent—
since the nature of pure deviation (*śuddhavyabhicāratva*) also exists therein, and thus it [the object] would [be designated] in that form— [nevertheless, ...].

Even though the consequence of an undesired result (*iṣṭāpatti*) might arise if [the definition] were a defect (*doṣatva*), nevertheless, since the inclusion of "not being composed of another qualified entity" (*viśiṣṭāntarāghaṭitatva*) in the definition entails the acceptance of a rule that it must indicate the property delimiting the object of the injunction (*uddeśyatāvacchedakadharma*) in that specific form, [this applies] to the word "defect" (*doṣapada*).

It should be noted that since the state of being a "deviation qualified by cognisability" (*meyatva-viśiṣṭa-vyabhicāratva*) is not such [a state], there is no resulting undesirable application of such conventional usage. Now, [one might object]:

is it not the case that the "obstructiveness" (*pratibandhakatā*)—which is defined by an "obstructedness" (*pratibadhyatā*) delimited by some property whatsoever that is pervaded by such "either-or-ness" (*anyataratva*)—...

If it is stated that "that which has a subject-object relation (viṣayitā) delimited by a certain form (yadrūpāvaccchinna) pervades [the subject-object relation of the inferential cognition] is a defect (doṣa) delimited by that same form," then there is no fault. In reality, however, the term "inferential cognition" (anumiti) here refers to a collective cognition (samūhālambana-anumiti) in which both the probandum (sādhya) and its pervaded reason (hetu) are the objects to be enjoined (vidheya) regarding the locus (pakṣa). Thus, there is no fault.

There is no fault [in this]. By incorporating as the definition the state of being sublated (*pratibadhyatā*) which pervades the nature of such an inference (*tādṛśānumititva*), it is possible to avoid the fault by taking into account a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-anumiti*).
Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) should be incorporated both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); therefore—
Since there is no failure to include either of the two—commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) or non-conclusiveness (*anupasamhāritva*)—he says: "In some cases...

In the root text, regarding the phrase "of such a probandum" (*yādṛśasādhya*), with reference to what is the designation of a fault applied to whatever property-qualification (*dharmāvacchinna*) when a formal argument (*nyāya*) is employed for the sake of an inference whose object is a subject and a probandum qualified by that property?
The meaning is that "established by tradition" (saṃpradāyasiddha) refers to the general definition of the fallacy therein, namely, mutual exclusion (anyānyatva).
By this, there is no harm even if the inferential cognition "the mountain is fiery because it possesses smoke" is unestablished (aprasiddha). And thus:

Even in the conventional usage, "there is a sublation (bādha) as a defect in the proof of Mount Vaḍabhimukha," this [usage] occurs through a desire whose object is an inference characterized by having Mount Vaḍabhimukha as its qualificandum (uddeśya) and fire (vahni) as its predicate (vidheya).

The meaning is simply that, in the application of a formal argument (*nyāyaprayoga*), there is a sublation (*bādha*) by any one of those [three types]. Although the definition is over-pervasive (*avyāpta*) in cases such as "the object of cognition (*prameya*) is like the sky," because an entity distinct from the object of cognition that is not possessed by the absence of the sky is unestablished (*aprasiddha*),
even if the properties are introduced as being any one of them, this remains the case in instances where the subject-locus (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is the object of cognition.

The state of non-establishment remains as before. Furthermore, since the property of being other than that which is both distinct from the absence of water and distinct from lake-ness is common to mere lake-ness, there would result the undesirable consequence of the conventional usage "the lake is a defect.
Nevertheless, in whatever [locus] delimited by whichever property...

There is no fault [in our position] because we intend to define a defect (*doṣa*) as a property that serves as the locus of the complete distribution (*paryāpti*) of the delimination (*avacchedakatā*) of the nature of being the determiner (*nirūpakatā*) of any one of the various objective contents (*viṣayitā*) delimited by those respective [properties]. Even in cases involving a single defect, it should be understood that the "any one" (*anyatama*) is established through the distinction between the qualifier-qualified relation (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) and its respective pervasions (*vyāpya*).

In this definition, since there is an absence of the conventional usage of "defect" (*doṣa*) with respect to fallibility (*vyabhicāra*) and the like when qualified by "knowability" (*prameyatva*), the condition of "not being composed of other distinct [qualifiers]" (*viśiṣṭāntarāghaṭitatva*) need not be included at all.
Now, one might object that such a general definition would apply commonly to two different defects in certain cases.
Since the fivefold division of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)— which is common to all three types of defects— is not established in some cases, he says "the wind," and so forth. Thus,
the division into five types is made precisely with reference to the general definition of the defect pertaining to each respective instance.

The state [of being]. Regarding the phrase "in some cases": the inclusion of the property of "subsisting in the similar instance" (*sapakṣavṛttitva*) in the definition "that which [subsists] in the similar instance and in the dissimilar instance" is purposeless, because it would result in the undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) that a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is actually an inconclusive one (*anaikāntika*). Even though the locus (*dharmin*) is one, the qualified entity differs due to the difference in its qualifiers.

The meaning is that the classification [of fallacies] is justified because there is no overlap (sāṃkarya) in terms of the objective content (viṣayitā) within the cognition of the obstructing factor. Regarding the phrase "in the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) component that constitutes pervasion (vyāpti)":
this refers to the state of being co-located with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya), provided that it does not exclude what is other than the locus of the probandum (sādhyavadanyāvṛttitva).

This is with the intention that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the pervader; however, if pervasion is understood as the co-occurrence of the pervader, then the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) [reason] should be understood as that which is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence that is co-occurrent with itself.
This is because it should be noted that the cognition of that absence alone constitutes the sublation (*pratibandhaka*) of the cognition of the [pervasion].

There is no possibility of it being a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) based on a single cause; for, since the cognition that [the reason] does not reside in a locus possessing the proven property (*sādhya*)—

such as the cognition that it resides in a blue pot— is not an obstacle to the cognition of co-occurrence with the proven property (just as the cognition of "having a pot" is not), there is an absence of the seed of defectiveness, and thus [the reason] lacks the character of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇya*).
The sense is that it is untenable for [the reason] to be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Now,
if a reason whose probandum is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) were defective, then in order to establish the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) of that probandum,
the Naiyāyika tenet would have to be that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists merely in the co-occurrence with the pervader (*vyāpaka-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Anticipating the objection that [this] is contradictory, he says: "It is purely positive" (*kevalānvayī*). The word *pratibandha* means "the object of the apprehension of the subverting factor" (*pratibandhakagrahaviṣaya*), and its connection (*anvaya*) is with the meaning of the term "purely positive probandum" (*kevalānvayisādhya*), namely, a probandum that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvapratiyogisādhya*).

"There would be no distinction. Although the subject (*pakṣa*) being a locus of that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpyavat*) constitutes a "counter-thesis" (*satpratipakṣa*),

whereas "contradiction" (*virodha*) consists in the reason under consideration being the counter-correlative of an absence that pervades the probandum— thus a difference in their essential natures (*svarūpabheda*) certainly exists— nevertheless, just as in the case of the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) fallacies and so forth...

Even though they differ from one another, the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are considered a single type because the seed of their defectiveness (*dūṣakatābīja*) is one; likewise, even for the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*), since they constitute the causal complex for a contrary inference, they would be a single type of fallacious reason due to the unity of the seed of their defectiveness, which consists in their being an obstruction.

The meaning is as follows: by "positive concomitance" (anvayinā) is meant that which possesses positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti); by "negative concomitance" (vyatirekeṇa) is meant that which possesses negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti). Regarding the phrase "incapacity" (aśakti):

thus, the very fact of indicating incapacity is the seed of its being a fallacy (dūṣakatābīja), and it is distinct from contradiction (virodha); this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "to be understood" (bodhyau): [the opponent asks] "But if this is so..."

Since there is no common form (*anugatarūpa*) shared by these four, how can they be divided by a single form? If their division were based on being that which brings about the non-existence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvotthāpakatva*), then even the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacy would be included within this very group; therefore, he says: "by being any one of them. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the property that delimits the objecthood (*viṣayatāvacchedakadharma*) of the cognition whose objects are these four is intended.

By the phrase "useful for the conventional designation of *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced opposition)," it is indicated that in such cases there is merely the conventional designation of *satpratipakṣa* according to the ancients, but this is not a *satpratipakṣa* consisting of a defect in the reason (*hetudoṣa*). The expression "first presented" (*prathamopasthiti*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), [implying that the designation applies] only when there is a pair of equally strong conflicting inferential cognitions (*parāmarśa*).
It should be noted that this is because [the term] is used in a figurative sense (*avayavahāra*). There is no utility for [this definition] in the present context;

that is, there is no utility at the point when the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are being defined. Now, one might ask: "Since this very thing is the fallacious reason called 'counter-balanced' (*satpratipakṣa*), why is there no utility [in including it here]? To this [it is replied]:

He says: "Regarding 'presence' (upasthiti)": two contradictory cognitive reflections (*parāmarśa*) act as obstacles to the effect of a reflection by their mere existence in their own nature (*svarūpasat*), not by being known. Since a reason-defect (*hetvābhāsa*) consists only in that which, when known under a certain form, obstructs inference, this [case of two conflicting cognitions] cannot possibly be a reason-defect.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "it indicates": [one might object] that, according to the view of the author of the *Ratnakośa*, since the cognition of a locus as possessing the absence of the probandum (*tadabhāvavyāpyavatājñāna*) does not act as an obstacle to the cognition of the locus as possessing the probandum (*tadvatājñāna*), it would be impossible for there to be a mutual obstruction of inferences in the case of a *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced opposition).

To dispel the objection that there is unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in having to postulate that the combined cognitions of "possessing the pervader of the absence of this or that" and "possessing the pervader of that," both of which have established capacities for producing certainty, are the causes of doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya), he says: "klṛpta... (established).

The meaning is this: for a given *parāmarśa*, the property of being an inference (*anumiti*) having that very [reason] as its predicate (*vidheya*) is the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), and not even the property of being a certainty (*niścayatva*), which is not a constituent of it. However, when each individual *parāmarśa* is present, there is an absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that would manifest an alternative possibility (*koṭi*).

In his view, there is no assumption of an additional causal relation [between doubt and the two cognitions], because determinate inferential cognition (*niścayātmikānumiti*) occurs when both subsumptions (*parāmarśa*) are present;
and when both alternatives appear as contradictory due to the force of the causes, doubt arises by implication. Thus, it says: "when there is recollection of both."

The point is this: since both alternatives of a doubt appear through the very same sensory contact (*upanayasannikarṣa*), when both alternatives—namely yellowness and whiteness—are presented, even due to the defect of jaundice (*pīta-doṣa*), there would only be doubt and not the ascertainment (*niścaya*) of yellowness. Regarding the term "excess" (*ādhikya*), it refers to the root text.
The point is that the "unestablished nature of being a pervader" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) is stated only in cases where the reason is something like "blue smoke" and so forth.

Here, both the absence of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum qualified by non-deviation, and its subordinates (*tadvyāpya*), should be understood as forms of *vyāpyatvāsiddhi*; they are subsumed under the category of "any one of these" (*anyatamatvena*). The seed of its capacity to invalidate [the argument] is...
[This refers to] being the delimiting factor of the obstructiveness to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor,

even if the seed of their defectiveness were identical, is it possible for them to be distinct fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because the Sage has taught *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy) and *siddhi* (establishment of the opposite) separately, just as he did for *bādhita* (sublated) and *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced).

The phrase "it is indicated" is to be understood as the ellipsis for "there is no intrinsic necessity (asvarasa). Regarding "because of its existence": the sense is that because blue smoke is not distinct from smoke in general, the pervasion (vyāpti) of smoke exists [in it].
The term "by way of non-limitation" is to be connected with "pervasion," and so forth. Regarding "by delimiting that": whoever...

The meaning is that a property (dharma) is a non-delimiter (anavacchedaka) when its absence [of the counter-positive] is delimited by that which is not its delimiter; for example, the absence of contact with a monkey in a tree is delimited by the root. This is because of the absence of being a delimiter.
Even though the root of that tree has a location that is not distinct from the location of the contact with the monkey residing in the tree...

The point is that it is precisely because there is an absence of the nature of a delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) consisting in a relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) that one accepts the absence of contact with a monkey on a tree at its root.

[This is said] because it would otherwise result in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). That which possesses the nature of a delimitor consisting in a relation of identity...

The point is this: if one accepts the absence of pervasion with respect to that specific delimitation, then even if there is no "useless qualification" (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*), it would follow that in all cases where a heavy property (*gurudharma*) serves as the reason (*hetu*), there is a lack of established pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).
Now, [one might object]: "But in all cases where a heavy property serves as the reason..."
Since it might be argued that "the unestablishedness of pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) is indeed accepted [as a fallacy]," he says: "Let it be so. Regarding the phrase "due to non-contradiction":

this is because it is admitted that even a cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatājñāna) which does not apprehend the state of being a delimitant of pervasion with respect to the factor that delimits its status as a reason, can still be a cause of inference; for this very reason.

The point is that even from a verbal *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration) such as "this possesses the pervader" (*vahnivyāpyavān*), where the property delimiting the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is not specified within the aspect of pervasion (*vyāptyaṃśa*), an inference is admitted to occur.
The author of the *Mīmāṃsā* school raises an objection with the words "And it is not [the case]... (*na ceti*). Thus, even in the case of the aforementioned *parāmarśa*...
The meaning is that an inference [of the form] "this is not pervaded by *viḍhddhic14* because it is pervaded by *vaḍhddhac14*" arises from another cognition, and not otherwise.

Even with that much—meaning even for the sake of precluding inference in the aforementioned instance—he concludes with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). This refers to the case where a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) serves as the delimiting factor of the probans (*hetutāvacchedaka*).
The ancient masters do not accept that there is a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) in all cases;

rather, they hold that this occurs only in instances where the property [in question] is constituted by another property that delimits its own co-presence (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) as a pervader. With this intention, he says: "In the case of a redundant qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇa*)."

Regarding the phrase "by way of excess": the sense is that since an excessive statement constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), the use of the word "blue" is superfluous when the statement "because of smoke" alone is sufficient.
By the phrase "of the probandum and so forth," [the author] refers to the locus which possesses the absence of the probandum and the locus which is other than that which possesses the probandum.

[This is] the inclusion [of the condition]. He states the result of including "not being produced by ordinary sense-contact" (*alaukika-saṃnikarṣājanyatva*) within the scope of the delimitor of the state of being obstructed (*pratibadhyatāvacchedaka-koṭi*)—namely, "at the moment following the cognition of sublation" (*bādhabuddhy-uttara-kṣaṇa*).
Thus, [it applies] when "extraordinary nature" (*alaukikatva*) is included within the scope of the delimitor of the state of being obstructed.

Regarding the phrase "the occurrence of a cognition qualified by that": the point is that since a cognition qualified by that [object] is not admitted even through ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-saṃnikarṣa*) following a sublating cognition produced by the same sense-organ, even the objection of "admitting the desired consequence" (*iṣṭāpatti*) is not possible here. "Extraordinary nature" (*alaukikatva*) means not being produced by ordinary sense-contact.

One might object: "When there is a non-locally perceptual (alaukika) valid cognition of absence, since a local sense-object contact with the counter-positive is impossible, a local cognition of its possessor cannot arise anyway; so what is the need for a separate relation of sublation and sublated in the case of the same sense organ? To this, he raises the following doubt: "Not so" (na ca).
Because it brings about the perception of the counter-positive; because it is possible to bring about that perception.

Having established the purpose in the case of an error regarding worldly non-existence, he states it in the case of valid cognition (pramā) with the words "where there is non-existence. "Conjunction" (samavadhāna)—and this [occurs] prior to the knower.

It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that, when such defects are present, the very possibility of a sublating cognition (*bādhapramā*) does not arise, because it is obstructed by the defect that produces the error regarding the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).
He states the purpose of including the qualification "not produced by a specific defect" as follows: "The conch-shell is not..."

"Yellow," and so forth. "Of mere error alone" means that error does not arise without a defect (*doṣa*); this is the intended sense. "In the case of a frog" means that through a defect consisting of the fat of a frog and collyrium, a perceptual error regarding a bamboo as being a snake arises; this is the intended sense. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), defects such as those of sorcery and mantras are included.
[The word] "compendium" (*saṃgrahaḥ*). [The phrase] "its manifester" (*tadvyañjaka*) means "the manifester of the universal of being direct perception" (*sākṣātkāratvajāti*).

If, by the statement "if it is established by experience," such an experience does not exist in reality, for what purpose should that be included in the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being sublated (*pratibadhyatā*) in a case involving the same sense organ?

It has been indicated [by the phrase] "the occurrence of doubt. The point is that since the property of being a cognition of a locus as possessing a feature—which is common to both doubt and certainty—is itself the delimitor of the state of being the counter-correlate (the object to be blocked), there is no separate status of doubt as a blocker. Thus, doubt produced by ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) is not possible at all.

Because it acts as an obstacle to the manifestation of the contradictory alternative— which is not incompatible with the causal complex of ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa-sāmagrī*)— otherwise,

doubt would arise even at the time of the certain cognition "the ground possesses a jar. Thus, how could there be the possibility of doubt produced by ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-saṃnikarṣa*) following the certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*)?

He explains with the words "the ground," and so forth. "In that case" means: when the causal complex of worldly perception belonging to one alternative acts as an obstacle to the manifestation of the opposite alternative.
"Even where there is no subsequent ascertainment of sublation" means: even in such cases, doubt would not arise.

The meaning is that there would be no doubt regarding the nature of a distant post, such as its being a post or something else. To the aforementioned objection, he states the acceptance of the position with "Om. "Not being worldly" means not being produced by worldly sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*). [This is because] when worldly sensory contact exists, all the alternative possibilities (*koṭi*) appear [in consciousness].

The meaning is: "because there is no subverting factor. Regarding the phrase "because both are possible": this means that in a state of doubt, it is possible for [the cognition] to be produced by ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) and also for a contrary alternative to appear. Even when ordinary sensory contact is present, its...

The meaning is that [the object] appears as a mere outline due to the defect of distance. By the phrase "it is explained in detail elsewhere," it is indicated that when there is an absence of any general defect that produces doubt, there is indeed a certain determination (*niścaya*) regarding the nearby object. The expression "according to the opinion of some" refers to those who do not maintain the view that the state of being a subject of inquiry (*pakṣatā*) consists in doubt.

This is the state of affairs. It should be understood that even for one who possesses certainty through verbal testimony (*śruti*), in this system the causal efficacy [of inference] is established solely as the cognition of the connection with the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is common to both certainty and the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*)—for the sake of validating the inference. Regarding the phrase "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) in the root text:

The meaning is: "that which has not previously apprehended the probandum as its predicate. Thus, in the case of the inference "Earth possesses odor, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades 'other-than-earth-ness,'" there arises—generated by the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consideration (*parāmarśa*)—a cognition of the difference from others residing in earth, which has the probandum as its qualificand (*sādhyaviśeṣyikā*).

The meaning is that this would result in the non-occurrence of inference. He introduces the subsequent refutation with the words "But [if you say] 'unestablished'... [and concludes] "it certainly does not occur. According to the Master’s (Ācārya) view, since the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) alone is the cause of inference in all cases, even by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*).
Since they accept that only positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) is apprehended,

and since inference from both types of consideration (*parāmarśa*) is unestablished, and because the nature of positive concomitance is constituted by the probandum (*sādhya*), at the very time of the cognition of pervasion—
The meaning is that the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) is necessary. Regarding the phrase "the inclusion of proof" (*siddhiparigraha*):

"proof" (*siddhi*) refers to the ascertainment of the probandum. Since there is no inference in the absence of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) when proof already exists, the term ending in "time" (*kālīna*) is included. Thus, in the case of inferring clouds from the thundering of clouds, [the definition holds].

He raises the objection—“And not...”—with the thought that since both doubt and certainty are absent, inference is accepted as occurring after merely a moment's delay following [the initial perception]; therefore, there is no inconsistency. The reading is “saṃśayotpatyaiva.”
The word "satī" (being present) means that immediately after hearing the thunder, because the husband— who possesses a non-apprehension [of the cloud] similar to the thunder pervading the clouds—
prevents the doubt whose alternative is the absence of the cloud; thus, due to this prevention,

there is no possibility of the manifestation of the alternative of absence through the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*), and consequently, the certainty arises by means of the mind (*manas*).

One might say, "Let it be so. But that being the case, since the established [conclusion] would act as an obstacle, inference would become impossible. If it is argued that this is postulated due to a momentary delay, the point is that inference could not be accounted for because the very subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) would have perished by then.

It should be noted here as well that the intermediate term (*antarapada*) is merely stated by oversight, because in the case cited previously, there was no prior doubt. And if one insists on the authority of this reading, then [the meaning of] the root text beginning with "without doubt" (*saṃśayaṃ vinā*) would be that at the moment of the arising of the *parāmarśa* through the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), etc., [prior to that...]

One should connect [the text] by assuming the intention that [inference occurs] due to the destruction of doubt, and by further postulating the intention that even in the case of the "thundering of clouds," inference arises immediately after the production of doubt.
Nor [is there a problem] if the cognition of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) is introduced simply as "cognition" (jñāna).

It should not be argued that there would be an obstruction to inference even at the stage when there is a certainty regarding the truth of the subject of the doubt; for this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). This is because even a doubt whose validity is ascertained regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is equivalent to a certainty regarding the absence of the probandum; otherwise, [the same would apply] in both cases.
The point is that, in this view, the inclusion of the property of being a certainty (*niścayatva*) itself results in the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

Regarding the phrase "not apprehending the absence of the object to be grasped" (*grāhyābhāvānavagāhinaḥ*): it refers to that which is delimited by whatever property the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) apprehends as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavatva*).

The meaning is: "not apprehending the absence of that which is to be proven" (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency even if the certainty regarding validity—namely, the cognition that "this [cognition] has the absence of the probandum as its qualifier"—apprehends the absence of the probandum in a locus where the probandum is absent. "Not a cognition of the absence of the probandum" means not a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding the absence of the probandum.

This is the meaning. It should be noted that this is because the opponent accepts that only the certainty regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) functions as an obstacle [to inference]. "Due to complexity" (*gauravāt*) means that the property of being a certainty whose qualifier is the absence of the probandum is more complex than the property of having the subject (*pakṣa*) as its qualificand. This is the sense.

Indeed, the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is precisely that which is delimited by a property such that the state of being a certainty whose object is delimited by that property—unassailed by the knowledge of invalidity—is a non-superordinate locus of the obstructiveness to inference. And this [property] is indeed common to the validity consisting in the state of having the absence of the probandum as its qualifier with respect to the subject under consideration (*prakṛtapakṣa*), wherein the probandum is absent; however, more on this...
He dispels the doubt that, according to the maxim "that which has already entered," such validity would be an *hetvābhāsa* (fallacious reason) even in your own system—
by stating "the subject possessing the absence of the probandum," and so forth. This is because [such a reason] is unfit to be a fallacy.
The word "tasya" (of that) from the preceding sentence is supplied [here]. Regarding the phrase "being presented first":

since the property delimiting the aforementioned counter-entitiness consists in the absence of truth (*pramātvābhāva*), it follows that, by way of being a cognition whose counter-correlate is known, it pertains to a cognition that is itself true (*pramātmaka-jñāna*).

The point is that since the cognition of the property that delimits the state of being an impediment (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka-dharma*) is required prior [to the cognition of the fallacy], it is appropriate for the "truth-status of the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāva-pramātva*) to be considered a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), by virtue of its being the first to present itself, as if due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
Regarding the phrase "contradiction, etc. (*virodhādi*): although it would have been more appropriate to say "inconstancy, etc. (*vyabhicārādi*), nevertheless...

It should be understood that, just as in the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), contradiction (*virodha*) also possesses a direct obstructive power against inference; however, for fallacies such as inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*), the obstruction occurs only at the stage of the *parāmarśa* (the subsumptive reflection), which is what is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). This is why they are described in that manner. By the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*), [this distinction is indicated].

The exclusion of the cognition that is useful for [establishing] the state of being an impediment. "Of that" means of the sublation (*bādha*). "Because it is impossible for it to have deviation as its object"—[this is said because] even though it is impossible for the cognition of sublation to have deviation as its object after the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*), the inferential consideration itself [is what is meant].

In response to the objection that there could arise a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) regarding the subject (*pakṣa*)—namely, "the subject possesses a reason that is pervaded by the probandum" and "it possesses the absence of the probandum," which concerns the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—he says: "in one [place]"; this refers to the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakābhāva*).
The meaning is that [the cognition] is a cause by virtue of occurring at the time of the effect (*kāryakāla*). This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);

it should also be understood that in one alternative (*pakṣa*), a cognition having as its object the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) which is non-pervaded by the probandum is impossible. Regarding the phrase "sublation and worldly [cognition]," [it refers to] within the scope of the delimitors of the state of being sublated by a contradictory cognition (*virodhijñāna*).

By including the condition of not being produced by worldly sensory contact (*laukika-saṃnikarṣa*), even a non-inferential reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) having a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolaka*) as its subject— just like a worldly sublation-cognition (*bādhajñāna*) regarding that same property— would subsequently give rise to a worldly perception whose object is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), namely, the existence of smoke in the absence of fire within that very iron ball.

The meaning is "it will come to be," and thus the point is that the subverting cognition (*bādhadhī*) indeed has deviation (*vyabhicāra*) as its object. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means "in inference" (*anumiti*).
Now, even in the absence of a lack of essential connection (*svarūpāsiddhi*), there is certainly deviation with respect to the time delimited by the moment of origination.

Since the property of earthhood (*pṛthivītva*) exists in a pot that lacks odor, he says: "non-occurrent in a different locus from the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). This is because if non-occurrence in a different locus from the counter-positive were not included within the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) that constitutes the deviation (*vyabhicāra*), [the definition would fail].

The point is that there would be the undesirable consequence of even a valid reason (*saddhetu*), such as "this is a tree because it is conjoined with a monkey," being subject to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Now, in order to avoid the consequence of such a valid reason being sublated (*bādhita*),

[the definition] must be restricted to a locus (*pakṣa*) and so forth that possesses an absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) which is non-co-located (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) with its counter-positive.

It must be accepted as a defect; for this reason stated above, in order to exclude the case of a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣitatva*), it must also be accepted that "counter-balancedness" belongs only to a subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses a pervader of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) that is non-co-locus with its own counter-correlate (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). As for the [definition of] the probandum...

Since there is no contradiction with the apprehension of a counter-reason (*satpratipakṣa*) when it possesses a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that includes the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) qualified by non-occurrence in the same locus as its counter-positive (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), the apprehension of the probandum is not opposed [by such a counter-reason]. Therefore, only a counter-reason whose pervasion does *not* include the qualification of non-occurrence in the same locus as the counter-positive is accepted; thus, the aforementioned valid reason (*saddhetu*) is not [invalidated].

"The state of being a subject (pakṣatva) possessing that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum"—this is not [correct]. For if that were the case, it would follow that in all instances, only the cognition of that which possesses the pervader of the absence [of the probandum]—as formulated without the condition of "residing in a different locus from the counter-positive" (pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya)—would be the sublater of the cognition of that [probandum]. And thus, previously...

This is because it is untenable for the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection), which is stated by the author of the treatise to be the cause of inference, to possess the property of obstructing doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*); for within the *parāmarśa* that is the cause of inference,
the object of cognition is precisely the pervasion (*vyāpti*) as constituted by the condition of non-occurrence in a different locus (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Therefore, since it is possible for that which pervades the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpaka*)— even when it incorporates a pervasion defined by non-co-occurrence with the counter-positive— to possess opposition to the probandum (*sādhyavirodhitva*),
it is appropriate that this alone constitutes a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*). And thus, in the case where there is odor in a jar delimited by the moment of its production...

"In that case, no sublation (bādha) is possible, because the absence of odor (gandhābhāva) in a jar is co-located with its counter-positive (pratiyogin). Do not say so; for where space and time possess the status of being the delimitors of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) by virtue of being relations of essential nature (svarūpasaṃbandha), there [the absence] is delimited by those [space and time]."

It should be noted that this is because the presence of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattva*) is also accepted as a form of sublation (*bādha*). Here, there is no counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*) either, because a property pervaded by the absence of odor—which is non-co-instantaneous with its own counter-positive—is impossible in a jar; for this very reason, this is an example of unadulterated sublation. Otherwise, it would be mixed with counter-balanced opposition.

In that case as well, sublation (*bādha*) would not constitute a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). It is not untenable for the state of being counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣatva*) to be pervaded by sublation, because there is no harm in a pervader (*vyāpaka*) existing in a wider domain. Nor is it the case that the mere absence of odor...
It should not be argued that, because [the absence of fragrance] is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) due to the absence of any relation [to its counter-positive],
it is possible here as well for it to possess the property of being pervaded by the absence of fragrance— where the pervasion is constituted by the counter-positive's non-coexistence—
and thus this too is merely a case mixed with a counter-reasoning (satpratipakṣa). For such a [reasoning]...

If one were to accept [the presence of] a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*), then even a valid reason (*saddhetu*) such as "a jar possesses fragrance because it is earth" would result in being considered defective; therefore, enough with this prolixity. "Thus is the reading" means that since a reading lacking that word is seen in some manuscripts, this has been stated. 71, 72. Further on as well...

Even regarding the definition of the "counter-example" (vipakṣa): the point is that the mere absence of the probandum (sādhya) does not constitute a counter-example; rather, the inclusion of the element of "certainty" (niścitatva) is for the sake of excluding fallacies. As for the phrase "is apprehended":
the remainder of the sense is that it is apprehended as the absence of proof (siddhi) qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā).

The section beginning with "sādhyaniścaya" and ending with "saṃbhavāt" constitutes the reason for [the mark] being a valid probans (*saddhetu*). Regarding the phrase "of the subject" (*pakṣasya*): thus, in the root text, the word *pakṣa* refers to *pakṣatā* (subjecthood), because it is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning; otherwise, [it would follow that] the absolute non-existence of space (*ākāśātyantābhāva*) is eternal...

It should be noted that there is no inconsistency [in the argument] because the reason "being an absence distinct from prior non-existence and destruction" (dhvaṃsaprāgabhāvabhinnābhāvatva) is not non-conclusive (anupasaṃhārin). Now, one might object: since doubt does not obstruct certainty, even if a doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya) exists everywhere, it is possible for a certainty regarding the probandum to occur in some cases; thus, the determination of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇyaniścaya) [would be established].

It is not difficult [to understand], and therefore he says: "at the time of the arising of doubt. This means even at that time, namely, during the state of certainty such as "the jar is denotable" (*abhidheya*). He says: "because there is no impairment. This refers to the fact that even at the time of such certainty, [one still entertains the doubt] "is everything denotable, or not?"
The sense is that because doubt arises, there is an absence of certainty due to the non-exclusion of all possibilities.
To the question, "But what follows from this?", he says: "And thus... [He explains: "Precisely by way of having the same mode of presentation (*samānaprakārakatvena*).

This is because there exists a certainty regarding the locus qualified by that [dharma] (i.e., the jar) as possessing the state of being denotable by the word 'jar', which is pervaded by denotability (*abhidheyatva*).
The sense is that there is an absence of the causal complex for doubt (*saṃśaya-sāmagrī*) with respect to that which is delimited by it. Regarding the phrase "by way of having a common object":
this means provided that the causal complex for a doubt having that as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) were to act as an obstacle to a certainty (*niścaya*) having that same qualificandum.
Now, [an objection is raised]: in cases such as "all things are nameable" (*sarvam abhidheyam*), [the probandum]...

One might argue that even if the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the property to be proven (*bhāva*) is not established, let the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth, when they are objects of doubt, be considered fallacious (*ābhāsa*);
therefore, he says "elsewhere" (*anyatra*). This is for the purpose of excluding fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire."

The sense is that, since only that which is delimited by a specific form (rūpa) whose being the object of a cognition constitutes a superfluous existence within the nature of the impediment to inference must be accepted as a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa), the probandum (sādhya) and so forth do not possess such a status. Now, one might object: even the cognition "this is smoke" possesses as its object a smoke-ness (dhūmatva) qualified [by other properties].
Since the pure [locus] is not distinct from the qualified [locus], he says "its own" (*sva*) for that reason— that is,
because it is the meaning of the word *antara* (interior/locus). However, if pervasion (*paryāpti*) resides in each individual [member],
then [the definition] consists simply in being non-different from that which is delimited by such a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) through the relation of pervasion.

In place of the argument regarding the non-substratum-ness of pervasion (*paryāptyanadhikaraṇatva*), it should be stated that this is because, just as in the case of being distinct from both [smoke and water],

there exists in the state of being mere smoke (*kevaladhūmatva*) a difference qualified by the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) that is pervaded by both the qualifier and the qualificand (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyobhayaparyāptāvacchedakatva*).

The object of meditation is the state of being excluded from what is other than fire. The sense is that since the application of the formal argument—"The mountain possesses fire, because it is excluded from what is other than fire"—is accepted by all, it is impossible for the desired conclusion (of proving the existence of fire) not to follow. Now, [an objection]:...

The state of not being constituted by another property in the capacity of the qualificand is simply the difference from that which is constituted by another property in the capacity of the qualificand.

Thus, although "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*) is a constituent of "blue-smokiness" (*nīladhūmatva*) in the capacity of the qualificand, "fireness" (*vahnitva*)—despite its exclusion from non-fire—is not a constituent of it in that same way. Therefore, [the definition] does not fail to apply.
Since it would follow that [the property] lacks the status of being a non-delimiter of pervasion (*vyāpyatānavacchedakatā*), he says: "of the difference from smoke and so forth.
By "being a delimiter of connection with the probandum" (*sādhyasaṃbandhitāvacchedakatvena*) is meant "being a delimiter of pervasion by the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpyatāvacchedakatvena*).
Pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) consists precisely in possessing such a property that is not a delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence co-located with itself.

The state [of being]. Regarding the phrase "it is an error": if it were [taken] as having a real object, then in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," at the stage of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "being composed of stone"—which is pervaded by the absence of fire—the fault of a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*) would be untenable for the ancients; therefore, even in that case...

The intended meaning is that this is because [the opponent] accepts the presence of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*). However, it should be understood that in a case where there is no contradiction between the probandum and the absence of the probandum, the technical designation "counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣa*) is not applied even if both types of consideration (*parāmarśa*) are present.
This is because there is no absence of the state of being devoid of odor (*gandhaśūnyatva*).
The meaning is: "because of the absence of the non-existence of odor, which has an unrestricted occurrence.

By this, there is no defect even if the absence of odor exists in the jar at the time of its production. This is provided that the word *pakṣa* (the subject) signifies that which is qualified by the delimiting condition of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

The sense is that, since the locusness (ādheyatā) residing in the absence of smell as determined by a jar qualified by its state at the time of production is unconditioned (niravacchinna), the subject (pakṣa) qualified by such an absence of smell constitutes a sublation (bādha). Alternatively, it means "because of the non-existence of the absence of smell," which is equivalent to "because of the existence of smell. Thus, [the reason] is "because of the presence of smell."

To this extent: thus, since sublation (*bādha*) consists precisely in the subject (*pakṣa*) possessing an absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) that is non-co-referential with the counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), the sense is: how can there be sublation here? Furthermore, if the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) has as its meaning that which is qualified by the delimitors of subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then in cases where space and time serve as the delimiters of subjecthood...

The point is that there is no inconsistency regarding sublation (*bādha*), because the presence of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) even as delimited by the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) constitutes a distinct form of sublation. Thus ends the chapter on Inference in the *Dinakarī-taraṅgiṇī*. [Regarding the phrase] "the connection by way of occasion" (*avasarasaṅgatim*):
*Avasara* (the occasion for discourse) consists in the fact that something must be explained immediately following [the previous topic] once the student's obstructive desire to know has been removed;

and in the present case, although both inference (*anumāna*) and comparison (*upamāna*) are dependent upon perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference is treated first because it is accepted by many schools of thought.

Since the desire to know first arises for one seeking proficiency primarily in inference— due to its ease of comprehension resulting from the absence of significant disagreement among minor disputants—
it follows that by defining inference, the obstructing desire to know is removed.

The sense is that since comparison (upamāna) must necessarily be discussed [after inference], its definition follows immediately after the determination of inference by way of "occasional connection" (avasara-saṅgati). Regarding the phrase "perception of similarity": if the instrument of comparison were nothing other than a cognition of similarity that is itself perceptual, then comparison would indeed be dependent upon perception.

It should be understood that the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) has been explained as referring to perception (*pratyakṣa*), with the intention that comparison (*upamiti*) is experienced immediately after ordinary perception whose object is similarity.
Regarding the phrase "this": it refers to the perception of the similarity of a cow in a gavaya.

The meaning is that it is designated as an instrument (*karaṇa*). He presents the traditional view with the words: "the verbal cognition of the meaning of the analogical statement" (*atideśavākyārthaśābdabodha*).

[He then says] "the recollection of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārthasmaraṇam*). The intention is that even that which produces it [the verbal cognition] is accepted as its operation (*vyāpāra*) by way of being an intermediate operation.

[Objection: But in that case, where there is a recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) due to another stimulant, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an analogy even without the perception of an object qualified by similarity.
To this, he says: "qualified by similarity" (*sādṛśyaviśiṣṭa*). [This is said] when disregarding the traditional view.

He states the seed [of the definition]: "by way of being a cooperative cause. He says, "it is logical," because the intention is that it would be cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate another instrument distinct from that. Now, if the perception of an individual object qualified by similarity constitutes analogy (*upamāna*), then it would be untenable for the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) to be its operation (*vyāpāra*), since only that which, while being produced by X, produces what is produced by X [can be considered an operation].

Regarding the objection that the statement in the root text— that the recollection of the meaning of the extended rule (*atideśavākya*) functions as the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*)— is inconsistent, because recollection, being an operation, is necessarily produced by an experience that possesses the same mode (*prakāra*) as itself:

He refutes this with the words "by similarity" (*sādṛśya*). Thus, although the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) is produced by a prior verbal cognition, the perception of a similar object (*sadṛśapiṇḍadarśana*) is also a cause there as a means of awakening [the latent impression]; therefore, there is no inconsistency—this is the intended meaning.

"By this" means by the description of the perception of a similar object (*sadṛśapiṇḍadarśana*)—which functions through the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*)—as being the instrument (*karaṇa*) of analogy (*upamiti*).

"Cognition" (*bodha*) means verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). "Because of its absence" implies that there exists only the meaning of the analogical statement in the form of a direct experience (*anubhava*). Now, if this is so...

Regarding the doubt as to what the instrument (*karaṇa*) and what the operation (*vyāpāra*) are in such a case—since the operation [of the sense organ] cannot be the cause because the verbal cognition is not produced by the perception of a similar object—the author demonstrates the instrument and the operation according to the view of a certain school (the *ekadeśin*), beginning with the words "But rather... and so on. [He states: "The mere cognition of similarity."
By the word "only" (*mātra*), the aspect of having the property of being a *gavaya* as its qualificandum is excluded. Regarding the phrase "both":

since both are produced by the cognition of similarity by way of being cognitions of qualifiers, these are the perception of the similar object and the cognition of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*).

The sense is that, because [the cognition] does not arise without comparison, and because both [the object and the means] serve as the instruments of comparison, there is no decisive reason [to prefer one over the other]. By the words "by this," he clarifies the point stated [earlier] with the passage beginning "where...
[he says] "because it is not accepted. Now, in this way...
Since the cognition of similarity (*upamiti*) is established by experience even in such cases, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of denying that experience; therefore, he says:
"But rather... (*kiṃtu*). [The phrase] "immediately after that" means that since the cognition of similarity can be accounted for with a delay of two moments, there is no need to deny the experience.

The state [of the matter] is as follows: "The gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'. Immediately after the visual contact with the individual body (piṇḍa), because the universal *gavayatva* is also grasped through perception due to its being present in a perceptible locus, the cognition of similarity to a cow has precisely that [universal] as its delimited subject (*dharmin*).

The intention of the root text is that even the cognition characterized by the qualifier "being denotable by the word *gopa*" is not untenable. As for the claim that the verbal cognition arising from the forest-dweller’s statement, "The gavaya is denotable by the word *gavaya*," because it resembles a cow, is itself *upamiti* (analogy) and not a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), this is not so.

It should not be argued that the object of the analogical cognition (*upamiti*) is precisely that the similarity with a cow is the delimitor of the denotation of the word "gavaya," and not *gavayatva* (the property of being a gavaya); for this is accepted [by the opponent]. He refutes that view with the words "by this" (*etena*).
The meaning is: because the analogical cognition has the form "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'."
"Without the apprehension qualified by *gavayatva*.
Even upon hearing the word "gavaya" as part of the aforementioned sentence, at that time, because the universal *gavayatva* itself is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),

and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to grasp the denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is qualified by it, [the word cannot function] by way of its primary signification (*vṛtti*).

The point is that, since the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the property "being a gavaya" (*gavayatva*) as delimited by the word "gavaya" is impossible, it is likewise impossible to have a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose qualificandum is delimited by that [property] and whose qualifier is "the state of being denotable by the word 'cow'.
Therefore, such an analogy (*upamiti*) must necessarily be a distinct type of valid knowledge (*pramiti*). Now, [an objection]:...

He raises the following objection: "And not [so]," meaning that we see no evidence for the claim that the analogical cognition (*upamiti*) has as its qualifier the state of being denotable by the word *gavaya* precisely as delimited by *gavayatva*, and not as delimited by similarity to a cow (*gosādṛśya*), which would necessitate that analogical cognition be a distinct type of valid knowledge (*pramiti*). This is stated in the phrase "in your view."

The remainder [is as follows]. However, it should be noted that in our own view, it is accepted that the analogy consisting of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) occurs precisely prior to the perception of the universal *gavayatva*. Regarding the phrase "due to its non-arising": an objection might be raised: "But surely, after the presentation of *gavayatva* by perception, there would be an obstruction caused by the cognition of its being cumbersome (*gaurava*), [and thus] with respect to the delimitation (*avacchedaka*) of similarity to a cow..."

Even if the cognition that "the word *gavaya* denotes [this animal]" is impossible [prior to perception], there is no obstacle to the arising of such verbal comprehension from the statement of a forest-dweller immediately before that perception;
therefore, he says: "from the word *gavaya*. And indeed, such [comprehension] is experienced from the word *gavaya*.
The meaning is that this is verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Now, one might object:

let it be granted that, for the sake of accounting for the verbal cognition whose qualifier is "gavaya-ness" (*gavayatva*) arising from the word "gavaya," the status of "gavaya-ness" as the delimitor of the denotability of the word "gavaya" is established through analogy (*upamiti*), namely, by the cognition "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'."

Nevertheless, there is no evidence that the verbal cognition arising from the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) apprehends the denotability of the word "gavaya" as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) specifically with the similarity to a cow;
for a verbal cognition apprehending the denotability of the word "gavaya" could indeed arise even with the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of similarity to a cow.

Because there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Nor should it be argued that the causal complex for the cognition apprehending "the denotability by the word *gavaya* as delimited by *gavaya*-ness" is itself the subverting factor in that case;
for such a cognition [requires] the cognition of similarity to a cow as having *gavaya*-ness as its locus to be its cause.

Since, at a time when *gavayatva* (the property of being a *gavaya*) is not presented through perception, the conditions for the apparatus of analogical inference (*upamiti*)— which consists of such a cognition— are impossible, it follows that by the force of the aforementioned verbal cognition alone,
the similarity to a cow (*gosādṛśya*) [is also established].
He raises the objection that the establishment of the property of being the delimitor of the denotation of the word *gavaya* is indeed free from obstacles—this is expressed by "not so" (*na ca*).
The phrase "due to apprehension" (*grahāt*) means due to apprehension consisting of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Even though such a verbal cognition has arisen, because the similarity to a cow (*gosādṛśya*) is cumbersome (*gurutva*), the property of being the delimitor of the denotation of the word *gavaya* [does not reside there].

He provides the resolution—beginning with "because it is sublated" (*bādhitatvāt*)—that because that [cognition] is an error (*bhrama*) due to having a sublated object as its content, the object is not established by it. [The author states: "Just like the perception of an individual object qualified by similarity, so too is the perception of an individual object qualified by dissimilarity... (*sādṛśyaviśiṣṭapiṇḍadarśanam iva vaidharmyaviśiṣṭapiṇḍadarśanam api*). This is because [the opponent] accepts the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

In some cases, it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in an analogy (*upamiti*). Here, the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the recollection of the meaning of the extended statement (*atideśavākya*), such as "the earth is denotable by the word 'earth' and possesses qualities unlike water and so forth. The resulting analogy is "the earth is denotable by the word 'earth'"; thus he says: "this is an illustration" (*upalakṣaṇam*). Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But surely..."

Comparison is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is possible to accept that the resulting cognition— "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'"— is merely a visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), being worldly (*laukika*) with respect to the aspect of the gavaya itself, and non-worldly (*alaukika*) with respect to the aspect of its being denotable by the word 'gavaya'. Nor is it...

It should not be argued that since an analogy (upamiti) is observed even when visual activity has ceased—by means of the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*)—visual perception is therefore impossible therein; for even so, there is no evidence that analogy constitutes a distinct type of valid cognition (*vijātīyapramiti*), as it could instead be an extraordinary mental perception (*alaukikamānasapratyakṣa*).
Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that [analogy] is attested by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I am analogizing."

Having established that valid cognition (*pramiti*) is of a distinct character, he establishes that comparison (*upamāna*) is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the instrument for that [cognition], beginning with "Now then" (*nanu*), etc. [He says this] because the cognition "I perceive directly" (*sākṣātkaromi*) does not arise;
for indeed, being an external object is what manifests the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkāratva*) for the mind, whereas the mind [is restricted] to external objects.
Since there is an absence of ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-saṃnikarṣa*), there is an absence of being an ordinary object;

thus, even though comparison (*upamiti*) is a form of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), it is possible for the cognition "I do not perceive [it] directly" to arise immediately thereafter, due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Otherwise, even after a non-ordinary mental perception regarding heaven, [one would likewise perceive heaven directly].

Because there would be the contingency of the cognition "I perceive directly," and likewise because of the cognition "I infer in this way," let the object [of comparison] be merely mental following the knowledge of similarity;
however, due to the underlying dissatisfaction that it is not a distinct type of valid cognition (*pramiti*), he says: "Otherwise... [and] "...of inference as well."
The sense is that it is possible for the very cognition following the sublating knowledge (*bādhajñāna*) to be the object of the reflective awareness (*pratīti*) "I infer.

And thus, just as in the case of the inferred object which becomes the object of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I infer" immediately after the valid cognition (*pramiti*), [the same applies here].
The meaning is that comparison (*upamiti*) is also the object of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I compare in this way.

Now, one might argue: let comparison be of the nature of a negative inference (*vyatireki-anumāna*), such as "the *gavaya* is denotable by the word 'gavaya' because it is similar to a cow; for whatever is not so [denotable] is not so [similar]," since there is the reflective awareness "I am comparing."

He dispels the objection that the object of the cognition of comparison (*pratīti*) might be an inference whose qualificandum is the capacity (*śakti*), by stating: "Nor [is it so], for this is the summary. This is because there is also the cognition: "I do not infer, I do not hear, I do not remember, but rather I compare (*upaminomi*)."
