The sense is that analogy (*upamiti*) is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramiti*). Thus ends the chapter on analogy in the *Dinakarītaraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Rāmarudra Sūri. [Regarding the phrase] "the relationship between that which is depended upon and that which depends":...
In this regard, according to the view of the ancients, the verbal cognition produced by the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*) itself constitutes the means of comparison (*upamāna*).

Since, in that system, the word (*śabda*) is produced by the knowledge of its meaning and the word alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there exists between verbal testimony and comparison a relationship of dependence (*upajīvyopajīvakabhāva*) in terms of their essential nature.

It should be understood that there exists a relationship of dependence between verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) and comparison (*upamiti*), because the latter is produced by a comparison consisting of the cognition of a capacity (*śakti*). However, according to the view of the moderns (*navīna*), who hold that comparison is simply the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśyajñāna*), the dependence of verbal comprehension upon comparison occurs through the mediation of the resulting comparison itself.

Some say that the intended meaning is that [the property of being produced by comparison] should be understood as residing in the word through an indirect (paramparā) relation consisting in its being the instrument of its own substratum. That is not to be trusted;
for the state of being produced by comparison—which consists in the cognition of similarity—resides in the resulting comprehension (upamiti) only through a direct relation.
Because analogy (*upamiti*) also has the nature of verbal cognition (*padajñāna*), it is essentially of the nature of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*);

thus, since the relation [between word and object] is possible by its very nature, one might ask: even if analogy is considered a form of verbal comprehension, since it too depends upon words regarding its object of comparison (*upamāna*), why is analogy not presented immediately after the investigation of verbal testimony?

Although it can be said that [this] has already been explained, there is no fault because the relation of connection (*saṅgati*) does not entail immediate mention [of what follows]. This has been elaborated upon precisely in the section on inference (*anumānakhaṇḍa*). Regarding the phrase "of that which has the meaning of the particle *eva*": the meaning is that which has the meaning of the particle *eva*.
The phrase "of which" (yasya) means "of that which indicates the meaning of the particle *eva* through a compound with the elision of the middle term.
Regarding the phrase "of hand gestures and so forth": thus, in cases such as the verses of the Muni (the Sage), and in cases of heterogeneous hand gestures, there is an absence of vocal utterance.

In the absence of a word being cognized, there would be no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). According to the view of the moderns (*navīna*), however, the cognition of a word is the instrument (*karaṇa*); thus, the point is that verbal comprehension arises from the cognition of a word as indicated by writing or by hand gestures. Regarding the phrase "of the mere cognition of the word-meaning" (*padārthajñānamātrasya*): although...

In the cognition of a jar and so forth through perception and other means, because there is an absence of being produced by the cognition of a word, it is impossible to speak of the cognition of the word as being its mediate operation (*vyāpāra*). Nevertheless, since the cognition "this jar is what is denoted by the word 'jar'" is also produced by the cognition of the word— by way of the proximity of application (*upanaya-sannikarṣa*)— [the word-cognition functions as a mediate cause].

It should be understood that the possibility of [the cognition] being an operation is established. The point is that for the verbal cognition "this is a jar," the quality of being produced by the knowledge of words is indeed easily obtained. Regarding the term "constituent" (*ghaṭakatva*):

it means that the state of being produced by a word—which constitutes the presentation of the word-meaning generated by the word—is [established] through the assistance of the relationship in the form of a *vṛtti*.
The root meaning is "that which is to be awakened" (bodhyam); the sense is that it is the object of awakening.
Now, if it is asked why the knowledge of the relationship in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) serves as a cooperative cause, the answer is as follows:
it is by way of the principle that the knowledge of one related member causes the recollection of the other related member.

The recollection of the word-meaning arises from the cognition of the word only when there is knowledge of the relationship between the word and its meaning in the form of a *vṛtti* (inherence or convention), and not from the mere cognition of the word alone. For instance, in the absence of knowledge regarding the relationship between an elephant and its keeper, one does not recollect the elephant even upon seeing the keeper.

It is necessary that the cognition of a relation must be assisted by the cognition of its relata. Thus, in the root text, the phrase "produced by a word" (*padajanya*) and so forth should be understood as "produced by the cognition of a word" (*padajñānajanya*) and so forth;
for it is precisely the cognition of one relatum that causes the recollection of the other relatum.

"Because of the absence of the presence [of the bank] [by means of the word itself]"—the meaning is this: since the relation between the flow (which is the primary denotation of the word *gaṅgā*) and the bank has already been apprehended, once the flow is presented by the word *gaṅgā*, the presentation of the bank is possible; therefore, one does not postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *gaṅgā* for the bank. Regarding the phrase "relation with either one":...
He dispels the misconception that this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound by stating "consisting of either one.

[The phrase] "only upon the presentation of the word-meaning generated by the word" [is used]; for in the absence of knowledge of the primary power (*śakti*), even the apprehension of *lakṣaṇā*—which consists of a relation to the primary meaning—is impossible, [and thus it applies] to both the word and the word-meaning.

Because, in the absence of knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning], it is impossible for the cognition of a word to produce the recollection of the word-meaning that serves as the cause of verbal comprehension;
and it is precisely with this intention that [the author] spoke of "the cognition of power" (*śaktidhi*) in the verse.

The intended meaning is that it has been stated that the cognition of the word functions as a cooperative cause [for the apprehension of the object]. Regarding the term "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*):

if the desire whose qualifier is "being cognizable by the word 'jar'" were the word-potency (*śakti*) of the word 'jar', then—since such a desire resides only in God—the word-potency of the word 'jar' would not belong to the jar itself.

It must be accepted that the denotative power (*śakti*) consists precisely in possessing such a desire related by the relation of qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*). Thus, because it would be cumbersome to postulate multiple desires for God, there is instead only a single manifestation of a desire in the form of a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*), namely: "The jar is to be understood from the word 'jar' and the cloth is to be understood from the word 'cloth'."

The point is that since it [the denotative function] must be accepted [as existing in all things], and since it exists in the cloth as well through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the word "pot" denotes the cloth. [The phrase] "because it also exists in the bank" means that because the Lord's will has everything that exists as its object, there is also the cognition of the bank from the word "Ganges" by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).
The meaning is that, because [the object] is being produced, its being the object of that [divine will] is also necessarily present in the divine will (*īśvarecchā*).
Thus, there is neither the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) nor the fault of the collapse of the definition (*lakṣaṇocchedaprasaṅga*),

given that [the definition] consists in possessing the divine will through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by the property of being the objecthood (*viṣayatātva*) of the cognition produced by that word.

By accepting that [the word] "pot" is denotative of that [object], since the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) determined by a qualifier-ness (prakāratā) delimited by the property of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "pot"— as specified by the will of God—
is absent in cloth and the like, it follows that cloth and the like do not possess the will of God through such a relation of qualificand-ness. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.

The point is that a cloth or similar object is the denotatum (*śakyārtha*) of the word "pot. Otherwise, since the Lord’s will would possess a qualifier (*prakāra*) where that [denotatum] is absent, it would follow that His will is erroneous (*visaṃvādin*). Furthermore, because there is no conventional usage of the word "Gaṅgā" for a riverbank and the like, [the Lord’s will] regarding that...
It is not accepted that the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" has the form "let the bank be the object";
rather, it is expressed in a dissociated manner, such as: "let [the bank] be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'Gaṅgā'," or "let the bank possess objecthood."
Because, by the will of the Blessed One, the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" is present in the bank; thus, in the bank and so forth,
[the relation] is the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the qualifier-ness (prakāratā) delimited by the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā."

The sense is that since the bank and so forth do not possess the status of being the primary denotation (*śakyatva*) of the word "Ganges," it is necessary to accept *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) in order to account for the verbal cognition whose object is the bank and so forth; this is established by the principle that [the secondary meaning belongs] only to that which is the qualifier of the qualifier.

The property of being qualified by the objecthood of the bank— which is the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" as determined by God's will in the form "Let the bank be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'Gaṅgā'"— resides in the objecthood of the bank; in that [objecthood], there is the property of being qualified by the objecthood of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā," which is delimited by the nature of being the objecthood of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā."

The objection raised by some— that the author’s statement is inconsistent because it is not accepted [that the relation is the qualifier-qualificand relation], but rather that it is simply the state of being determined by a qualifier delimited by the reality of the pure object— is without foundation.

Anticipating the objection that "there is no primary denotative power (*śakti*) in a name based on modern convention," which would contradict the root text— since the root text states that there *is* indeed power in a modern name—
the author explains that the phrase "in a modern name" refers to a specific type of name, beginning with the words "ādhunika" and so forth. In the root text, [it is stated] on the eleventh day...
The phrase "the father shall name him" must be supplemented by the words "according to the Vedic injunction. This is because of the existence of God’s will— specifically,
the Lord’s will which has as its object a cognition produced by a particular word that has been conventionally designated as such, and which takes that specific meaning as its qualificandum.

The meaning is "because it exists. Now, since even corrupt words are observed to have conventions in certain instances, it is not supported by evidence that the Lord’s intention is directed toward them in that form.
Furthermore, there would be the burden of postulating an infinite number of modes, qualificands, and individuals.
With this intention, he says: "occurring at the time of the eleventh day.

Thus, the intended meaning is that the postulation of the Lord's will takes the form: "Let the qualificand designated by the father and others become the object of the cognition produced by the word uttered by the father at the time of the eleventh day."

[Objection: Even so, the root text beginning with "but in the case of a name recently designated by convention" (*ādhunika-saṅketite tu*) would be irrelevant, because one accepts that the primary denotative power (*śakti*) resides in the name designated by the father and others on the eleventh day;
therefore, he supplies the word "only" (*mātra*)—namely, "only a recent [convention]" (*ādhunika-mātra*). By the word "only," God (*Īśvara*) is excluded.

The sense is that there is no harm even if there is a capacity (*śakti*) in those previously mentioned names, because the conventional designation of "Lord" (*īśvara-saṅketa*) exists in a general form. "Asvarasam" (dissatisfaction) means what will be stated hereafter. He reveals this dissatisfaction with the words: "If that were so," etc., beginning with "without error regarding capacity and without grasping at figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."
Even if verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) occurs through that [notion] of power, error, and so forth, there is no deficiency.

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication); for even among those such as the Prābhākaras who do not accept a Lord (*īśvara*), it is possible to grasp power in the form of the Lord’s will (*īśvarecchā*).

It should also be observed that the verbal cognition [of the sentence] would otherwise be untenable. In the root text, the phrase "dhātu-prakṛti" means "dhātu-prātipadika" (verbal roots and nominal stems).

"Pratyayas" refers to case-endings (*vibhakti*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and primary verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta-kṛt*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), compounds (*samāsa*) and so forth are included; for even in compounds and the like, according to the grammarians—

Because of the acceptance of [linguistic] capacity (*śakti*). In that regard, the grammar [of Pāṇini] is the means for grasping the capacity of roots such as *bhū* (to become) and *as* (to be). Furthermore, the capacity of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as *pācaka* (cook) is also grasped through grammar;
specifically, the fact that the root *pac* has "cooking" as its meaning is understood from the primary suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) following it.

And because the meaning of agency is established therein, it should be understood that in that case, the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of primary nominal stems such as *go* (cow) and others occurs through the lexicon (*kośa*) alone. In reality, the compound *dhātuprakṛti* means "that which has the form of a verbal root as its base" (*dhāturūpaprakṛti*). This demonstrates that the verbal root functions as the base (*prakṛti*).

And [the word "prakṛti"] is used precisely to indicate the distinction from the suffix (*pratyaya*). For this very reason, it should be understood that the inclusion of compound formations (*samāsa*) and other types of *vṛtti* is also intended by the term "and so forth" (*ādi*). In reality, the phrase "the base of the verbal root" (*dhātuprakṛti*) means "the base consisting of the form of the verbal root. Furthermore, the demonstration of the status of being a base (*prakṛtitva*) with respect to the verbal root is [intended] in contrast to the suffix.

This is solely for the purpose of illustrating the suffix *laṭ*. For this very reason, the inclusion of compound formations (*samāsa*) and other types of word-derivations (*vṛtti*) by means of the term "beginning with" (*ādi*) is also consistent; the essential point is that these too possess the status of nominal stems (*prātipadika*). The distinction is that rules such as "the suffix *laṭ* occurs in the sense of the present tense" serve to apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the suffix.

Regarding the phrase "of the universal *kṛtitva*": there is parsimony (*lāghava*) if a single, unqualified *kṛtitva* is the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), whereas there is complexity (*gaurava*) if infinite individual acts (*kṛti*) qualified by *kṛtitva* were the delimiters of the denotatum; for it is accepted that a universal alone appears in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*), not the individual act.

The sense is that if the delimitor of denotability were [the action] in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*), there would be prolixity (*gaurava*); for since it is accepted that only the universal (*jāti*) appears in its own form, it is impossible for the action to be the delimitor of denotability in its own form. However, according to the modern grammarians (*navīna-vaiyākaraṇas*), [it is the action] only as the substratum (*āśraya*).

In this view, the capacity (śakti) for agenthood and objecthood is accepted in verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), since the operation (vyāpāra) such as *kṛti* and its fruit (*phala*) are obtained by the verbal root alone, and substratum-hood (*āśrayatva*) is an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) upādhi; thus, there is no complexity (*gaurava*) in that system. However, it contradicts the fundamental sūtras such as "laḥ kartari" (Pāṇini 3.4.69).
Nor should it be said that the meaning of "kartari" (in the agentive) is simply "the locus" (āśraya);

for if that were the case, the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) formulated by the author of the Sūtras—"the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*)—would become redundant. [Therefore,] wherever the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is employed in this own system of grammar, its meaning is as follows:

It is precisely for the sake of making this known that there is respect for the technical rule (paribhāṣā). Furthermore, independence (*svātantrya*) consists in having an operation that is not dependent on the operations of other factors (*kāraka*); and this [definition] is indeed excessively cumbersome.
And thus: "The verbal root [denotes] the result and the operation, [and] the substratum..."

Furthermore, even the *kārikā*— "tu tiḍdtdh;ḥ smṛtāḥ"— is indeed in contradiction with the *sūtra*. Moreover, it must be admitted that the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) signifies the locus [of the action] only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since its primary meaning is simply that which possesses the volitional effort (*kṛti*).

And thus, it should be understood that, in comparison with that [alternative], it is better [to accept] the very *kṛt* suffixes themselves as having the nature of a connection through *lakṣaṇā*, because [otherwise] there would be a lack of uniformity (*ananugatatva*). This is by virtue of [the rule] belonging to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*). That is to say, it is read immediately after the sūtra containing the governing heading *anabhihita*.

The meaning is: "by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*" (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Having raised the objection, "What is the proof [for this]?", [the author states: in examples such as *caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("Caitra cooks rice"), it is only the number residing in Caitra that is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and not the number residing in the rice and so forth.

The final meaning [of the objection] is as follows: one might suspect that in cases such as *caitreṇa pacyate taṇḍulaḥ* ("Rice is being cooked by Caitra"), since the expression of the number residing in Caitra would be possible even in the absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would not occur. Regarding the phrase "not occupied by [the status of] objecthood, etc.": this refers to that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*).

As for the word *iti*, its purpose will be demonstrated later at the very root [of the discussion] in the context of the usage "he cooks the rice" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), where the second case ending has no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the status of being an object (*karmatva*); in that case, the purpose is to prevent the connection of number (*saṃkhyā*) with the rice. And this is not [the case] when the status of being an object and so forth is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*).
It should not be argued that the second [form] alone is incorrect because of the rule "dvitīyā karmaṇi" (the accusative case is used for the object);

for even if it were incorrect, there is no obstacle to demonstrating its purpose, since there is no restrictive rule stating that only a correct usage must be shown as having a purpose. This is true even in the case of corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*).
It should be understood that this is because, through the arising of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is possible to produce a verbal cognition with respect to that [object].

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, however" (*nanu*): when "not being subsumed by [other] karmas and so forth" means not being a qualifier of the meaning of case-endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*) such as the accusative, then [this applies] in cases such as *caitra iva*.

Even though [the term] "similarity of meaning" (artha-sādṛśya) is a qualifier— as in the case of Caitra— [the number denoted by] the verbal suffix would still apply to Caitra as well as to Maitra, because it is not a qualifier with respect to the objecthood (karmatva) and so forth that constitute the meaning of the kāraka-case ending. Therefore, [the author] defines [the required condition] as "not being occupied by objecthood and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: if "not being subsumed under objecthood (*karmatva*) and so forth" means "not being connected with objecthood and so forth," then in cases such as *pakvam annaṃ bhujyate* ("the cooked rice is eaten"), the number expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) could not be connected with the rice, which is already connected with being the object of the act of cooking (*pāka*). Therefore, this [definition] is necessary; this is the intended meaning.

It should be noted that, in this way, it would be improper to abandon the claim that [the word] is not the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*) by virtue of being associated with other [meanings]. Now, one might object: "The term 'karmatva' (objecthood) and so forth, which denote other meanings, is redundant; for by employing the term 'unobstructed' (*anavaruddha*), which signifies not being the intended object as a qualifier, [that purpose is already achieved]."

He states that the intended meaning is that the entire collection [of attributes] is not the object of the qualification, because it is not restricted by being a *karman* (object) and so forth, due to the natural sense of the word "sāmañjasyāt" (from consistency). He says "in reality," however, to address the following objection:
"But surely, having abandoned the state of not being a qualifier of the other, [it must be taken as] a qualifier of the other."

In order to dispel the doubt that pursuing [the fact that something] is not the intended object of the purport is fruitless, he states "the state of being without qualification" while showing its purpose: "in another, the meaning of the particle *eva*. The meaning of the particle *eva* is threefold.

There are three types: the exclusion of connection with another (anyayogavyavaccheda), the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda), and the exclusion of absolute non-connection (atyantāyogavyavaccheda).

Among these, when the particle *eva* is connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), its meaning is the exclusion of connection with another; for example, in "Caitra alone cooks" (*caitra eva pacati*), there is the exclusion of the status of being an agent of cooking in anyone other than Caitra.

In that context, the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from another [person] and the exclusion itself possess distinct capacities within the particle *eva*. However, the meaning of "another form" appears as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the portion pertaining to Caitra. Furthermore, the relation, which is precisely the application (*prayoga*), is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the action denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
In the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) consisting of the absence of such a connection, [the object] occurs as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*);

and that absence appears in another [object] as a qualifier (*prakāra*). Thus, the form [of the cognition] is: "Caitra possesses an effort conducive to cooking; [and] one other than Caitra possesses the absence of a relation to an effort conducive to cooking."

Thus the verbal cognition arises. And so, it is also refuted that in the aforementioned instance, because the relation is a *kevalānvayi* (universally positive), the non-existence of the relation (*saṃbandhābhāva*) is unestablished, and consequently the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) itself would be impossible.
Furthermore, the meaning of the particle *eva* when conjoined with a qualifier is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). As for example:

In such cases as "The conch is indeed white," the non-connection of whiteness with the conch is excluded. Furthermore, when the particle *eva* (indeed) is connected with a verb, its meaning is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). For example: "A lotus is blue."

In such cases as "it certainly exists," the absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) of the blue house with the lotus is excluded, but not its mere non-connection (*ayoga*). This is because, in some lotuses, even the absence of the relation of blueness exists; this is how it should be understood. For although [the term] "absolute" (*atyanta*) applies even to non-connection, [it is used here to exclude the possibility of connection].
Alternatively, it must be stated that [the property] is simply the pervader of being a lotus (*sarojatva*), since anything else is difficult to specify;

and thus, because the absence of a relation with "blueness" (as a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in a lotus) is unestablished, its exclusion is difficult to achieve. Nevertheless, even in the case of non-connection (*ayoga*), there is the quality of "extreme" (*atyantatva*).

The meaning of the term "absolute non-connection-exclusion" (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) is precisely the exclusion of the state of not being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of difference residing in the lotus; thus, the aforementioned inconsistency does not arise.
Now, it may be argued that [the object] is simply not the intended referent of the speaker's intention by virtue of being a qualifier distinct from the meaning of the particle *eva*.

It must be stated that [the referent] is not subsumed under [other] kārakas such as the object (karman). Consequently, even though the meaning of the particle *eva* functions as a qualifier for something other than Caitra himself, there is no logical inconsistency in the connection of number with him; for this very reason, the word "other" (*itarat*) is also meaningful.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Caitra," etc. Here, the meaning of the accusative case is "object-ness" (*karmatva*).

The point is that, because Caitra is the object of the speaker’s intention as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of number with Caitra. [The phrase] "merely by being a qualifier" means: being the object of the speaker’s intention as a qualifier, while not being the object of the speaker’s intention as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*).

The point is that the absence of that [other meaning] is the regulator for the connection with a specific number. Now, one might object: in cases such as the word *saindhava*, which has multiple meanings, the understanding of salt at one time and a horse at another must be regulated; therefore, it is only in such instances that the knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) serves as the cause for determining the meaning, and not in all cases involving words with a single meaning.

Since there is no reason to assume that [the number] has that [the denoted object] as its cause, one might raise the following objection with the words "And if... and so forth: in cases such as "like Caitra," when there is no intention to treat Caitra and the like as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) of the meaning of the suffix *iva*, then the number would have to be construed with Caitra and the like. [The author replies: "In cases other than those involving multiple meanings (*nānārtha*)."

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Even in the absence of actual intention (*tātparya*), since a cognition of an erroneous intention is possible, one must observe that even if the cognition of intention were a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) in general, there would still be the undesirable consequence of the number (*saṅkhyā*) being construed with Caitra. Regarding the phrase "at that time," etc.: it serves as the sole determinant of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*).

In expressions such as "like Caitra" (*caitra iva*), the term "non-qualification" (*aviśeṣaṇatva*) is intended here to mean precisely that which is not presented by the nominative-case word *caitra*. Thus,
in the case of "like Caitra," the nominative-case word *caitra* functions solely as a qualifier for the meaning of the particle *iva*.

Because it is that which is to be presented [as the subject], number does not apply to it. In examples such as "Caitra alone cooks," the word *mātra* (alone/only) is used to justify the application of number to Caitra. The state of being a "mere qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatvamātraprayojakatva*) consists in being a cause for the status of a qualifier while not being a cause for the status of being the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣyatva*). Although...

Even in cases such as "like Caitra," when the recollection of the referent produced by the word "Caitra" occurs, Caitra appears precisely as the primary qualificand; thus, even that [word] does not have the function of being merely a qualifier. Nevertheless...

No fault whatsoever arises here, as what is intended is merely the state of being the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) as determined by verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Nor should it be argued that the mention of "ending in the nominative case" (*prathamānta*) is redundant;
for in the sentence *caitraḥ caitraṃ paśyati* ("Caitra sees Caitra"), the word *caitra* ending in the accusative case (*dvitīyānta*) [would otherwise be excluded].

Because it is necessary to include that [qualifier] in order to ensure the application of number (*saṃkhyā*) to Caitra— since he is presented as the qualificand merely by virtue of being the motivator of the qualification— it would follow that even in a case such as "Caitra cooks;
Maitra is as beautiful as Caitra," [the same problem would arise].
It should not be argued that in that case, where there is a collective verbal cognition (*samūhālambana-śābdabodha*) produced by two sentences, the number (*saṃkhyā*) would fail to apply to Caitra,

because at that time the property of being presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta-pada*) of that specific kind is indeed present. [This is incorrect] because, wherever a verbal cognition arises from a word ending in the nominative case and a verb (*ākhyāta-pada*) such that it possesses a cognitive object (*viṣayatā*) characterized by a mutual relationship of being the determined (*nirūpaka*) and the determined-in-itself (*nirūpya*), which is brought about by those two words themselves...

In that case, it is established because it is accepted that the absence of being presented by the first-case-inflected word which functions solely as a qualifier is the condition for the application of the number denoted by the verbal suffix; thus, in the aforementioned instance,
there is no [application of number] from either the verbal suffix in *pacati* or from the word *caitra* occurring in a different sentence such as *caitra iva*.

Since such a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is produced, there is no inconsistency regarding the application of number (*saṃkhyānvaya*) therein. Therefore, it should be understood that even those specific words found in the text are properly consistent. Now, [one might object]:
in the sentence "He cooks the rice-grains" (*taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), with respect to the factor of the rice-grains being the object (*karmatva*), [how is this explained?]

In the absence of the intention to express [the base-meaning] as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), the accusative case alone is not justified; for the rule "the second case is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) prescribes the accusative immediately after [the base] only when there is an intention to express the base-meaning as a qualifier with respect to the factor of objecthood (*karmatva*). Thus, [the statement] "there is no intentionality regarding the status of being a qualifier" [is established].

The root [of the problem] is unconnected; therefore, he says: "Not in the case of being a qualifier," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of being a qualifier and the primary qualificand," etc.:

where the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the verbal cognition is "the one who possesses an activity conducive to the cooking of rice is Devadatta," then, in order to prevent the application of number (*saṃkhyā*) to the rice (*taṇḍula*) as well, [the restriction is necessary].

The intended meaning is that [the rule applies] to that which ends in the nominative case, and so forth. Now, one might object: "In the sentence 'He cooks the rice-grains' (*taṇḍulān pacati*), when there is an intention to convey the aforementioned cognition, it is precisely what we desire that the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) should also apply to the rice-grains. If one were to say this, then [the author replies] regarding another instance, such as the mention of "that which ends in the nominative case," etc.
He demonstrates the purpose [of the definition] with the words "this" (*idam*). Thus, in examples such as *caitra iva* ("like Caitra"), the phrase "karmatva, etc.

(*karmatvādi*) is included to exclude the application of number (*saṅkhyā*) to Caitra. In examples such as *caitreṇa supyate* ("Caitra sleeps"), the phrase "ending in the first case," etc. (*prathamāntatvādi*), is included to exclude its application to the act of sleeping; this is also the purpose for employing the term "correct" (*sādhu*).
The sense is that it arises in this very manner. Regarding the phrase "of the second member":

in the sentence *taṇḍulaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), when there is an intention for the operation (*vyāpāra*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), to be construed as a qualifier of the rice (*taṇḍula*), then number is construed only with that which is the locus of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

In that case, the connection with number is also necessarily required. Thus, when the number is expressed, the nominative case (prathamā) is also necessary; for, according to the rule "when both [the nominative and accusative] are applicable, the latter [case-role] prevails," the nominative expressing the agent whose function has already been denoted is stronger than the accusative. And so it is.

The usage "Caitra cooks rice" (caitraḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati) is grammatically correct, just like the usage "Caitra sees Caitra" (caitraścaitraṃ paśyati). However, in reality, according to the rule *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ* ("the agent [who is also the object] is treated like the object"), since the status of being an object is extended to the agent who is non-different from the object, the suffixes *yaK* (passive marker) and *ātmanepada* endings are mandatory; thus, one says *pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*.

The construction *svayameva* alone is correct. The meaning is that, with the intention of demonstrating that the use of correct forms (*sādhuprayoga*) itself is the very purpose [of the rule], the purpose of [the requirement] "ending in the nominative case" (*prathamānta*) and so forth has been stated in order to exclude the application of number (*saṃkhyānvaya*) to adverbs of action such as *stokam pacati*.

The state of being a *bhāvanā* consists in being either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*). It should be noted that: "The ablation (*apādāna*), the recipient (*sampradāna*), then the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as well as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*)—this is the recognized order of the *kārakas*. Regarding the phrase "ending in the second case":
by the *Vārttika*, "Accusative status and neuter gender apply to adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa)."
The sense is that because the accusative case is prescribed for objects (*karma*) and because adverbs (qualifiers of action) end in the accusative;

"to be understood" (*vibhāvanīyam*) means that even in this alternative view, being unoccupied by [the categories of] objecthood and so forth consists simply in not being the intended referent of the speaker's purport merely by virtue of being a qualifier distinct from the meaning of the verbal root.

The intended meaning is that it is what ought to be expressed. "Without taking the connection with number as its object" means that in examples such as *dārāḥ santi* ("there are wives"), the plurality inherent in the meaning of the verb is sublated by the meaning of the word *dāra*, which is always used in the plural; this is the intended sense. And thus, regarding *la*:

In the term *kartṛ* as well, because the word *kartṛ* is a designation where the state [of being] is primary (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśa*), its meaning is precisely "agency" (*kartṛtva*). And agency is primarily the possession of an effort conducive to an action;
secondarily, it is the possession of an operation conducive to an action, or simply the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*), as in cases such as "it perishes" (*naśyati*).

It should be understood that "counter-correlativity" (pratīyogitva) is also [implied]. Thus, under the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "when not already expressed" (*anabhihite*), even in rules such as "the third case-affix is used for the agent and the instrument" (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*), the meaning is precisely "for [the meanings of] agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*)," and so forth. Where there is objecthood (*karmatva*) or agency (*kartṛtva*)...

Furthermore, the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) is expressed there by the nominative case alone, not by the second or third cases; for the rules prescribing those cases—such as "the second case after an object" (karmaṇi dvitīyā)—fall under the governing heading of "when not already expressed" (anabhihite). Thus, when there is a desire to express the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) as the primary qualificand (mukhya-viśeṣya), it occurs in the vocative.

Because the nominative case is prescribed only for that which is the substratum of agency and so forth expressed by the verbal suffixes (lakāra) and so on; by this [principle], it follows that the non-expression of the number residing in that [agent] by the verb is precisely what necessitates the use of the third case in the word following the expressive term, as in "dārāḥ santi" and similar instances. By the verb [in such cases],...

It should also be understood that the objection—that because the plurality [of wives] is sublated and thus not conveyed, the instrumental case ending in *dāraiḥ* would result—is refuted. Regarding the phrase "because of being produced" (*janyatvāt*):
the point is that the meaning of the term "operation" (*vyāpāra*) is precisely that which, while being produced by something, is itself the producer of what is produced by that thing.
"Even in its absence" means even in the absence of effort due to the chariot being insentient.

"Of the activity conducive to motion" means that the meaning of the verbal root *gam* (to go) is an action conducive to conjunction with a subsequent location. The chariot is precisely the locus of that [action].

The meaning is that in expressions such as "the chariot goes," [the action] is perceived in the chariot itself, and not as the state of being connected by ropes or the like to horses and so forth which possess the corresponding activity.

"Nirūḍhalakṣaṇā" (conventional metaphorical indication) means a metaphorical indication that has been the object of intention since time immemorial. "And so forth" (ādinā) [refers to other such cases].

And thus, although there is no restrictive factor for the lakṣaṇā (indirect indication) of the ākhyāta (verbal suffix) as denoting the substratum (*āśrayatva*) in the case of "he knows" (*jānāti*), the restriction certainly exists in cases such as "he desires" (*icchati*) and "he exerts effort" (*yatate*). This has been stated by accepting that words such as "Caitra" denote the self as delimited by its respective body. Caitra...

If, in accordance with usages such as "fair-complexioned" (gauraḥ), "emaciated" (kṛśaḥ), or "well-proportioned" (sacchāyaḥ), these [words] refer to the respective bodies [of the individuals], then it must be understood that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) signifies the delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Now, he explains the manner of verbal cognition (śābdabodha): "of the kṛt-suffixes" (kṛtām); this means "of the kṛt-pratyayas."

Regarding the word "artha" (meaning): the ellipsis is "but not [the meanings of] agency or objecthood. In cases such as *caitraḥ paktā* ("Caitra is a cooker"), let there be no cognition of identity-based relation; for it is possible for the agency and so forth denoted by the *kṛt*-suffix to be related to Caitra and the like simply as its locus (*āśrayatā*). Therefore...

He says: "Of the name and the object. This means: of the objects of names other than particles (*nipāta*). By this, there is no fault even when, in cases such as "the jar does not exist," the jar and so forth are construed with the negative meaning (*nañartha*) through difference (*bheda*);
for [such a construction] is unestablished (*avyutpanna*) in the sense of a relation other than identity (*abheda*). "Through difference" means by a relation distinct from identity.

The meaning is: "because of the absence of expectancy" (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*). Even if one were to accept that expectancy exists for the cognition of the relation between a name and its referent, there would be no cognition of a relation of difference in cases such as "the ground, a jar" (*bhūtalaṃ ghaṭaḥ*); therefore, he says: "the details elsewhere."

The point is that it is more appropriate to assume that the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the cognition of a distinct relational connection (*bhedānvaya*) is solely with the meaning of the suffix along with the meaning of the nominal stem, and not even with the meaning of the nominal stem itself; for this assumption is simpler than the alternative of postulating that the co-utterance of those [suffixes] with their respective [nominal stems] serves as the cause for the cognition of a distinct relational connection.

"Because it apprehends the expressive power (śakti)": the sense is that the locative case [in "kośe"] signifies being the denoter, and denotative capacity consists in the nature of expressive power (śaktatā).
"In terms of possessing blue and so forth": this means with respect to colors such as blue, yellow, and the like. "Precisely by virtue of its brevity": [this refers to the definition of *jāti*].
Rather than postulating that the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) belongs to an infinite number of specific forms such as "blue-ness" and so forth,

it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) for a single universal such as "blue-ness" to be the delimitor of denotability by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); since it is possible for a universal to manifest by its own nature, it is thus [the delimitor] in its own form.
The meaning is that there is no sublation [of the rule]. Regarding the phrase "from words denoting qualities" (*guṇavacanāt*):

the grammarians who composed the grammar intend the elision of the suffix *manu*, which expresses the sense of "possessing that" (*tadasyāsti*) and is prescribed after words such as *nīla* that denote qualities.

The collective meaning [of the sūtra] is: "because of the grammatical tradition (smṛti) stating 'from a word denoting a quality which has this as its meaning'. And in this regard, in all cases such as "there is a blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭo'sti*), rather than relying on the postulation of a lost suffix expressing the sense of the possessive suffix *-matup* prior to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), [the quality is directly related to the substance].

It is more appropriate to assume that words such as "blue" (*nīla*) have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to that which is qualified by the form "blue" and so forth. Furthermore, for a person who has not remembered the suffix *matup*, there would be no verbal cognition; yet, such verbal cognition is indeed experienced even when the suffix *matup* is not remembered following the knowledge of that specific word-order.
Thus, the lack of intrinsic plausibility has been indicated by the two [objections] beginning with "apivadantībhyām. Regarding the phrase "knowledge of the effect" (*kāryajñāna*):

the meaning is "knowledge having the effect as its qualifier (*prakāra*) through the relation of identity (*abhedasaṃbandha*). Although it would be more appropriate to postulate the expressive power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), because that [state] occurs as a qualifier (*prakāratayā*) in cases such as "bringing a jar" (*ghaṭānayanādi*).

Since the fetching of a jar can be accomplished simply by bringing it within the range of perception (*bhānopagama*), it is improper to postulate a power (*śakti*) for words toward those [objects] which are infinite in nature as the substrata (*dharmin*) of the effects;

this is because such a postulation is redundant (*gaurava*). Therefore, the statement that the capacity of words is determined to produce a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the effect through non-difference (*abheda*) is inconsistent. Nevertheless...

The Prābhākaras maintain that verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) has as its object the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) through the Vedic indicative mark (*liṅ*) and other means by virtue of its being a "thing to be accomplished" (*kāryatva*). Here, an objection is raised: since the *apūrva* was not previously presented [to consciousness], it is impossible to grasp the word's denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to it.

However, according to these very same [logicians] who do not accept the existence of universals (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), just as in your view a verbal cognition regarding previously unexperienced cows and the like arises from words such as "cow" when their denotative power has been grasped with respect to a cow experienced in a certain way— by virtue of the fitness (*yogyatā*)— so too in my view does it occur in the case of jars and the like by virtue of their being effects (*kāryatva*).

This is because it has been established that even in cases such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), where the potentiality (*śakti*) is grasped through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is the *apūrva* (unseen potency), by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*). This is due to the fact that in the case of an effect in the form of a jar or the like, the property of being produced by a sacrifice (*yāgajanyatva*) is sublated; therefore, [the cognition] must refer to the *apūrva*.

It should be noted that this is what was stated by the phrase "the cognition of the effect. It must be understood that, because [the universal] functions as the power (śakti) and so forth, the capacity (śaktatva) is accepted as residing specifically in the word that serves as the delimitor of the incapacity (*aśakyatāvacchedaka*) for something else;
for in that case, it is impossible for the power to be either undelimited or singular. And thus, further on...
The meaning of the root text, "verbal cognition having *kāryatā* as its object," should be understood precisely as "verbal cognition having that which is delimited by *kāryatva* as its object.
Regarding the phrase "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*): [it refers to] the conceptualization of multiple causal powers (*kāraṇatā*) restricted to each specific word-form (*tat-tat-pada*).

The meaning is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate to assume that causality is restricted to being a word (*padatva*) rather than being dependent on [the individual phonemes]. "Experiential" (*ānubhāvikī*) means that which generates the experience of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). "Power" (*śakti*) means capacity (*sāmarthya*). According to that view, [this power belongs] to words.

Power (śakti) is twofold: the recollective (smārikā) and the experiential (ānubhāvikī). Among these, the recollective power resides only in things such as a jar that are not connected to an action. And thus, from words such as "jar," the mere recollection of the jar and so forth is established. The experiential [power], however—

It should be understood that [the capacity for producing verbal cognition] resides only in words such as "jar" when they are connected with an action (*kārya*). Now, an objection might be raised: even in cases such as "The jar is blue," where there is no suffix such as the optative (*liṅ*), since individual words alone possess the causal efficiency for producing a verbal cognition whose object is connected with an action, such a verbal cognition would indeed arise.

To the objection that [the injunction] must necessarily be so, he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). The point is this: since the production of an effect by its cause requires the cause to be qualified by a pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) when it is already qualified by a pervaded property (*vyāpya-dharma*), there can be no such verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) without an optative suffix (*liṅ*) or the like. [The compound] *kāryatvāviṣayaka* means "that which does not have 'being an effect' (*kāryatva*) as its object."

Even that which has "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) as its delimited object is described in this way because it has "the state of being an effect" (*kāryatā*) as its object. Likewise, it should be understood that even that which denotes something qualified by "the state of being an effect" is called "denoting the state of being an effect" precisely because it denotes the state of being an effect. Regarding the phrase "by this": it means by the aforementioned method.
The meaning is: "by means of the introduction of this book. Regarding the phrase "the occasion for the power of remembrance" (*smārakaśaktiprasaṅga*):

the intention is that grammar and other sciences were introduced in this present work precisely as the means for grasping the power of remembrance (*smārakaśakti*). [Regarding the word] "of words" (*padānām*).

The meaning is "of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. It should be understood that this is because words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) lack the presentation of their own produced effect. Regarding the phrase "first of all" in the root text: it means prior to the knowledge of parsimony (*lāghava*) with respect to "jar-ness" as a verbal object (*śābdatva*), in comparison to "jar-ness" as a verbal object associated with an effect (*kāryānvita*). This introduces the view of the Bhaṭṭas.

The meaning is that he refutes that view. If one were to admit that an object not presented by the words appears in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then in cases such as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*), there would be the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition having cloth (*paṭa*) as its object;
therefore, the rule must be accepted that only an object presented by the words appears in verbal cognition. And thus:
However, since words do not present the relation between two word-meanings, such a rule would be violated;

therefore, the Bhaṭṭas maintain that the power of words resides in their being related to something else (anvita). In this context, "something else" refers to another word-meaning, and "related to that" means qualified by a specific relation having that other meaning as its correlate, such as a jar.

The meaning is that the word-potency (*śakti*) belongs to words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*). In this regard, since the other [relatum] is obtained from another word itself, the potency of words like "pot" is not accepted as including that [other relatum] within its own denotation; rather, it resides precisely in the pot and so forth as qualified by those respective relations, which are characterized by having the other [relatum] as their counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

The intention of the root text is that even the Bhaṭṭa view is indeed unacceptable, because the property of having an "associated pot" (*anvitaghaṭādiviṣayakatva*) as its object is more complex than the property of having a "pot" as its object (*ghaṭaviṣayakaśābdatva*). Nor, in this way, [is there any problem] from such [sentences] as "the pot exists."

It should not be said that there is the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding objects such as cloth [arising from a sentence like "Bring the pot"]. This is because [the causal relation] holds: with respect to a verbal cognition delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition possessing a specific object-locus (viṣayatā) distinct from the relation-ness (saṃsargatā), the cause is an object-presentation (upasthiti) generated by a word which does not have that specific object as its content. For that which is not presented by a word enters into the verbal cognition only through the roles of qualifier (prakāra) or qualificand (viśeṣya).

Because [the relation] cannot be manifested [by the individual word-meanings]. However, the manifestation of the relation in verbal cognition is governed precisely by a specific expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of two words;

thus, there is no lack of regulation in that regard. Furthermore, in accordance with the maxim that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise," a primary denotative power (*śakti*) is not admitted for the relation, because the relation is obtainable through expectancy. This is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "of the word *yava*": this refers to the maxim of the "lamp on the threshold. Just as a lamp situated on the threshold connects both the interior of the house and the external world by illuminating all objects therein, so too the aforementioned word ending in the genitive case connects both the previously grasped power (*śakti*) and its subsequent application.
The meaning is that [it] follows as well. In the root text, beginning with "tatra hi," he explains the manner of the connection. Regarding "tatra hi":

the meaning is "in the case of [the sentence] 'yavamayaścarurbhavati' (the sacrificial oblation consists of barley). With the intention that the requirement for a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) in determining capacity occurs only in cases where there is doubt, he says "tādṛśa" and so forth.
He completes the sentence with "tādṛśa" (of such a kind). With "tadvācaka" (denoting that), the meaning is:

because there is no word that directly denotes [the relation of] denotative power (*śakti*). However, in the lexicon (*kośa*), in passages such as "Vināyaka is the king of obstacles," the locative case conveys the sense of being a denoter; and since denotative power (*vācakatā*)...

The intended meaning is that there certainly exists a word expressive of that [power], since power consists in being the determinant (nirūpakatā) [of a relation]. Furthermore, it should be understood that in cases such as "Amaras, Nirjaras, Devas," these words have the capacity to convey the power [of a meaning] through the ellipsis (adhyāhāra): "These words denote the same object."

Regarding the phrase "of a word whose meaning is already established": even the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word whose meaning is already established is a means of grasping word-meaning (*śakti*) by way of inference alone. Thus, from the aforementioned sentence, the cognition arises: "In this mango tree, that which produces sweet sounds is denotable by the word *pika*. Prior to [this], regarding the word *pika*...

It should be understood that because there is no prior apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*), the apprehension of that power occurs solely through inference following the sight of a cuckoo: "The cuckoo is denoted by the word *pika* because it is the agent of sweet-sounding on the mango tree.
Regarding the phrase "by way of occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*), the meaning is "due to the connection of the occasion" (*prasaṅga-saṅgateḥ*).

"Without having grasped [the qualifier]" (nāgṛhīta): the logical principle is that a cognition does not arise with respect to a qualified object when the qualifier has not been grasped. By the etymological analysis "that by which the qualifier has not been grasped"—meaning it has not been made an object—a cognition that does not have the qualifier as its object does not arise with respect to the qualified; that is to say, it does not become a cognition whose object is the qualified.

Because the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) has the sense of being an object (*viṣayatva*). "On account of parsimony" (*lāghavāt*): the meaning is that there is parsimony in postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) in the single, pure property of potness (*ghaṭatva*), rather than in various pots qualified by potness. "The qualificand," etc.: [this refers to] denotation (*abhidhā*).
The word-power [does not] go to, that is, does not reach, the qualificand. To the question "Why?", he says: "exhausted.
After the phrase "the power of the qualifier is exhausted," the word "being" (sat) is to be supplied. Thus, because the word-power, having reached the qualifier—

The meaning is that its power being exhausted and its capacity being spent, the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) would not reach— that is, it would not attain— the denotation; for, according to the method to be explained,
the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding the qualified object arises from the word itself which possesses the power to denote the qualifier.

The sense is that there is no basis for postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the qualified portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*). Two objections against accepting a power in the individual (*vyakti*)—namely, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and infinity (*ānantya*)—have been stated in the root-text. Having raised these two as alternatives, he refutes them by means of the phrase "yasmāmiti" (in which...).

Regarding the phrase "because of deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*): it must be stated that for a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having a particular object as its content, the cause is precisely the knowledge of the expressive power (*śaktijñāna*) residing in that [object] as its qualificandum (*dharmika*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of a verbal cognition of a cloth (*paṭa*) arising from the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), and so forth. And thus, [the power resides] in a single individual pot (*ghaṭavyakti*) alone.

The point is that if one accepts the word-potency (*śakti*) for the word "pot," then because a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding another pot would arise, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in such a causal relationship [between the potency and the cognition].
He states the refutation of the second alternative: "infinitude" (*ānantyam*), meaning if one were to accept potency in all individual instances (*vyakti*).

The sense is that the second objection follows from the fact that because individuals are infinite, their expressive powers (śaktis) must also be infinite. In the root text, having raised the doubt that if there is no power residing in the individual, the manifestation of the individual in verbal cognition would be impossible, it is stated that the individual is manifested because the manifestation of the universal (jāti) is impossible without the individual.

That is not consistent; for where there is a recollection having "cowness" (gotva) as the primary qualificand, the manifestation of the universal (jāti) is possible even without the individual (vyakti). Likewise, since the manifestation of the individual in verbal cognition is impossible without the causal complex that manifests the individual, he explains that passage [beginning with] "jāti" as follows: [The text continues: "The word 'jāti' is used in the sense of the universal, while the word 'ādi' includes the individual and so forth.
