"Because it is the cause. Thus, the meaning is that the cognition of the power (*śakti*) having the genus (*jāti*) as its qualificandum is what makes the genus appear in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); that very same [cognition] is also what makes the individual (*vyakti*) appear. "Produced by the word": because, with respect to a verbal cognition having a certain object, the apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by a word having that same object is the cause.

Since the apprehension of the relation occurs only between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), the cognition of one relatum in the form of the word leads to the recollection of the other relatum in the form of the universal alone, and not of the individual. Consequently, because there is no recollection of the individual produced by that [cognition], the verbal comprehension of the individual cannot be established; therefore, with respect to the individual...

The meaning is that capacity (śakti) is necessary. Now, one might object: even if one accepts that a word has a secondary function (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the individual (vyakti), how can both [the individual and the universal] be considered functions, given that there is no recollection of the individual produced by the word through primary denotation (śakti)? This is the sense of the question. The phrase "as stated before" means in the form of the undesirable consequence of infinite denotative powers (śaktyānantya-prasaṅga).

"By way of not being followed" means by way of not being delimited by properties that are both pervasive and non-overlapping. Regarding "the impossibility of delimitation": [this refers to the view that] if such a single property existed in the individuals, then for a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by that [property], [the cause would have to be] a knowledge of the expressive power (śakti) having as its qualificandum that which is delimited by it.

The meaning is that, because causality is possible, when the causal status resides in the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*), it is the power itself— acting as the object— that can serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), and not the absence of such a property.
Nor can it be argued that the knowledge of the power regarding a particular object should be the cause for the verbal cognition regarding that same object.

This must be stated; for if that were the case, there would be the impossibility of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) regarding an individual cow or the like that has never been previously experienced and is not the object of a knowledge of the word's power (*śakti*).

This is the intended meaning. He demonstrates how it is possible for an individual to serve as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) within the causal efficiency residing in the knowledge of the power—given that individuals are subsumed under the universal "cowness" (*gotva*)—with the words "And thus... (*tathāca*).
"In the verbal cognition of the word 'cow' (go-śabda-bodha)" means: a verbal cognition whose object is delimited by cowness (gotva).

"In all cases" means: there is no evidence for [the claim that] in general, with respect to a verbal cognition having a certain object, the cause is the mental presence (upasthiti) produced by a word having that same object.

"Because it has already been stated. Thus, the point is that for one who lacks the knowledge of the word "pot" having a denotative power (śakti) with respect to potness, the occurrence of a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding a pot is not possible.
Nor, even in this case, does the presentation of potness produced by the word [occur] through the assistance of such a knowledge of power...

The meaning is that this is because [the knowledge of the relation] is accepted as being the cause of such verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, the knowledge of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is not a direct cause of verbal cognition, but rather functions through the medium of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*);
therefore, there is no deficiency even if the knowledge of the expressive power is absent in all cases immediately prior to the moment of verbal cognition.

Furthermore, as for the phrase "what then": [an objection is raised]—even if the cognition of a linguistic capacity (*śakti*), namely that "the word 'cow' has the cow as its denotable object" (*gaur gopada-śakyā*), is a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), the existence of a linguistic capacity in the individual (*vyakti*) is not thereby established. This is because it must be admitted that the aforementioned cognition is erroneous; and according to the maxim, "a thing is not established by means of an error," [the capacity does not reside in the individual].

He says: "‘Cow’ and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the impossibility of verbal cognition": the intention is that since the knowledge of the relationship in the form of a *śakti* (potency) exists only between the universal *gotva* and the word ‘go’, it is only the cognition of *gotva* that can be accounted for as a recollection (*smaraṇa*), and not the individual (*vyakti*) as well;
it is with this in mind that the [status of the individual as] recollection is set aside. As for the phrase "in whichever part": [it refers to the specific aspect].

The meaning is: "the aspect which is the locus of its own property. In the phrase "that aspect" (*tadaṃśa*) as well, the meaning is "the aspect which is the locus of that property. Both instances of the word *tat* refer to a single property.

Thus, a cognition having "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth as its qualifier, which has its own locus as its object, [serves] only with respect to verbal cognition having "cowness" and so forth as its qualifier and its own locus as its object.

The meaning is that if "cause" refers to the capacity (*śakti*), then there would be the impossibility of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having "cowness" (*gotva*) as its qualifier with respect to the individual (*vyakti*), because the capacity itself is the locus of cowness. This is the sense of the phrase "in whichever part," etc., according to its literal meaning.

That is not possible; for if that were the case, it should be understood that the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding an unseen potency (*apūrva*) as an object—arising from the knowledge of the capacity (*śakti*) of a jar and so forth as delimited by "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—would be untenable, as will be explained later. This refers to those Prābhākaras. [The phrase] "having a universal as its qualifier" (*jātiprakāraka*) means as follows:

The meaning is that there is unity of power (*śakti*) in that very [individual], because simplicity (*lāghava*) is possible through the possibility of its being undifferentiated (*niravacchinna*). For this very reason, even by them, the power of the word *paśu* is accepted as residing only in the individual qualified by hair, a tail, and so forth, and not in the tail alone.

It should be understood that this is because they are infinite in number and because it is impossible for them to manifest in their own specific forms [simultaneously]. Regarding the phrase "not opposed by erroneous cognition": since the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists only between two cognitions that are qualified by a sublating factor (*bādha*) and share the same delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), a cognition of power whose subject lacks such a delimiting property [is not so opposed].
The intended meaning is that [the opponent] accepts [the word] as being the cause [of the cognition]. However, this is contrary to experience;

for at the time of the subverting cognition that "cowness is not the denotatum of the word 'cow'," even for one who apprehends cowness as having the nature of cowness, [the cognition does not arise] from the word "cow."
This is because of the intention that a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) whose object is the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is accepted by some [authorities].
Although a cognition in the form "this is a cow," which has cowness as its qualifier (*prakāra*) in its own right (*svarūpataḥ*),

is not [the intended meaning] because it is obstructed by the subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) "this is not a cow," [this is so] regarding the aspect of the expressive power (*śakti*) in its own right.
Even the word "cow" (gopada), which has "cowness" (gotva) as its qualifier, is not incapable of denoting cowness;
thus, it is indeed sublated by a contrary cognition. Therefore, it is not necessary for cowness to be a qualifier specifically in its aspect as "cowness-ness" (gotvatva);
nevertheless, the universal (jāti) exists in its own right only through inherence (samavāya).

It is accepted as a rule that [the relation] is through the relation of manifestation (*prakāratva*) and not through any other relation; otherwise, there would result the linguistic usage "the pot is knowledge," just as one says "knowledge is a quality. This is because potness exists in the cognition by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*); however, in the case of the word-meaning (*śaktyaṃśa*), cowhood exists only through the relation of being contained (*ādheyatā*).

Alternatively, the modehood (*prakāratā*) must be expressed; thus, the intended meaning is precisely that the manifestation of cowness must be admitted as being solely through the form of cowness (*gotvatva*). And in this way, by the etymological derivation "that in which contrary cognition is not obstructed," [the term *aviruddha* is explained].

"Of that which is not obstructed by contrary cognition" means "of that which is not contradicted by contrary cognition. Regarding the first cognition, the reason for its being unobstructed is its having no determiner of the locus (nirdharmitāvacchedakakatva).
For the second, however, the reason for its being so is simply the non-establishment of anything to be obstructed (pratibadhyāprasiddhi).
It must be analyzed as follows: "the establishment of the property of being the delimitor of denotability.

Nor should it be argued that the object of the cognition is merely the co-existence (*sāmānādhikara�ya*) of the denotability with the nature of "cowness" (*gotvatva*), and not its being delimited by that [nature] as well; for such cognitions...
Since the property of "apprehending a qualified-qualifier relation" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhitva*) is the general rule,

it is inappropriate to abandon it; for in the cognition of a qualified-qualifier relation, it is accepted that the qualifier and the qualified appear through relations such as being delimited (*avacchinnatva*), with the delimitors of the qualifier and the delimitors of the qualificandum being dependent upon the substratum (*dharmi*).

[This is] the state of affairs. And as for [the phrase] "not": it should be noted that this is a doubt raised by bystanders, and not by the Prābhākaras themselves, because the latter do not admit the existence of error (*bhrama*). Now, it may be argued that between a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*bādhaka*), there is indeed a fixed rule regarding which one is the sublater; and in the present case, there are infinite individuals...

The very complexity of including [the property] within the scope of the delimitor of possibility remains indeed an obstacle to the cognition of the qualificandum. In fact, in the case of a cognition of qualified-qualificandhood (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya-bodha*),

it is precisely in the aspect of the relation that there is a sublation of the state of being a counter-correlate delimited by the delimitor of the qualifier and the state of being a substratum delimited by the delimitor of the qualificandum.

It is not accepted that [the universal] is a qualifier in the manner previously stated, because that would result in the cognition having a different form; for this reason, he says "let it be so" (*astu vā*), out of a sense of dissatisfaction.
Regarding the phrase "of the objectivity of the cow" (*goviṣayatāyāḥ*): this is because the nature of "cowness" (*gotvatva*) has a constitution that is itself composed of the cow.

[Objection: Since the root [of the word] is taught to have its denotative power (*śakti*) residing in an individual qualified by both genus (*jāti*) and configuration (*ākṛti*), it follows that both genus and configuration are the delimiters of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). That is not tenable.

Because of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is appropriate that the denotative capacity (*śakyatā*) be restricted to the genus (*jāti*) alone. Nor should it be argued: "Since it will be stated later that there is only one single denotative power across all three [the individual, the genus, and the form], and since the property of 'cowness' (*gotva*) does not subsist over the entire extension of the denotative capacity, how can it possibly serve as its restrictor (*avacchedaka*)?"

Because it is possible for [the property of being the denotatum] to serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) with respect to the qualified denotability (*viśiṣṭa-śakyatā*), since it pervades the denotability qualified by its occurrence in individuals (*vyaktivṛttitva-viśiṣṭa-śakyatā*) and because it is not over-extensive (*anatiprasakta*) with respect to the denotability delimited by pure denotability (*śuddha-śakyatātva*). Otherwise, both...
Even if [the property] were the delimitor of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), that defect would remain as it was. Thus,

even if the three possess a single power (*śakti*), the fact that one is presented as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and another as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) must be explained— in both philosophical systems— solely through the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

The meaning is as follows: "state" refers to the configuration of parts (*avayava-saṃsthāna*), which is the conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*). Regarding the phrase "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):

the meaning is that in the case of a capable [individual] cow, the conjunction of parts exists precisely through the relation of coreferentiality. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for the pure universal of cowness (*gotva-jāti*) depends upon the conjunction of parts.

One should also consider that there is parsimony (lāghava) in postulating a single genus (*jāti*) as the delimiting factor for various individual manifestations of conjunctions, rather than postulating such a factor for each individual manifestation. Regarding the phrase "only one":
this is because from words such as *hari*, which possess multiple powers (*śakti*) and multiple meanings, there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of each individual meaning separately.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "the singular number," the intention of the author of the Sūtra is that there is indeed a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) when the oneness denoted by the singular number constitutes the referent of the word, in the form of the word's own expressive power (*pada-śakti*). The term "one" (*eka*) is to be supplied immediately after the phrase "in the individual qualified by the universal" (*jāti-viśiṣṭa-vyaktau*); otherwise, [the argument would not hold].
It should be noted that even in the case of a generic form (*ākṛti*), there is no possibility of the particle *eva* [implying restriction] precisely because a distinct capacity is admitted for it.
Now, an objection may be raised: there can be no mutual cognitive connection (*anvaya*) between the referents of two words;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a mutual connection even between the horse and the sun, which are the respective referents of the word *hari*. Nor [can this be avoided] by [asserting] a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*).

It should not be argued that there is no fitness [for connection] and an absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the relation by way of difference, because it is unestablished that the meaning of two nouns can be related through difference;
for if that were the case, even the generic form (*ākṛti*) could not be related to the individual (*vyakti*) as its substratum.

Therefore, since it must be accepted that there is no expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) when the relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*) occurs between the two objects presented by the two names, he says: "due to linguistic usage" (*vyutpatti*). And thus, even if there is an absence of expectancy elsewhere when two word-meanings are related to one another, [the relation still holds].

The point is that, just as in the case of the meanings of the particle *eva*, a syntactic connection and expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) are postulated for both the form (*ākṛti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) in accordance with actual experience. Now, even if this were so, one might object that the singular number in the Sūtra would be untenable because there is no unity of power (*śakti*) among the three; to this he says: "That which belongs to the Sūtra."
"They say" indicates the presentation of a lack of logical consistency (*asvarasa*). The seed of that [objection] should be understood as follows:

if the capacity (*śakti*) resides in the delimitor of the referent (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), then because singularity (*ekatva*) would be sublated, the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the singular number would be untenable. Incidentally, he states the delimiters of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) for words such as "that" (*tat*) and so forth: "of the word *tat*," and so on.

The "speaker" is the one who utters that word. The meaning is that the speaker’s power (śakti) resides in that word as uttered by him with respect to that which is delimited by the property of being a jar (ghaṭatva) and so forth, which serves as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the status of being the object of the speaker’s cognition. Although, on the grounds of parsimony (laghava), it would be more appropriate to state simply that [the power resides] in "that which is present in the mind," nevertheless, in cases such as "he exists" (so'sti) and so forth...

It should be noted that even complexity (gaurava) has been accepted for the sake of accounting for the cognition of a jar as a "jar" which is established by experience. Regarding the phrase "the consequence of a difference in powers" (śaktibhedāpatti):

the sense is that if there were a difference in powers, it would follow that words such as *tad* (that) and others would also possess multiple meanings; and this is not an acceptable consequence (neṣṭāpatti).

If that were the case, then by the maxim "that which is uttered once [denotes its own meaning]," there would be the impossibility of understanding both a jar and a cloth simultaneously in expressions such as "those two" (*tau*); furthermore, the intention is that in the section on polysemous words, the referents of pronouns like *tad* and so forth have not been stated. [The phrase] "because of the consequence of their manifestation" means...

The point is that in the verbal cognition produced by words such as "cow" (*paśu*), properties like "having hair" (*lomatva*) and "having a tail" (*lāṅgūlatva*) are observed to appear in that manner. And in the present case, in expressions such as "that [jar] is non-existent" (*so 'san*), the verbal cognition established by experience is precisely "the jar is non-existent," and not otherwise.

It should be understood that there is no possibility of an "unwanted consequence" (iṣṭāpatti), because [the cognition] has the form "that which is delimited by the delimitor of the object-sphere of the intellect exists. Regarding the phrase "as a secondary indicator" (upalakṣaṇatayā):

being a secondary indicator means being a subsumer of the state of being the delimitor of the denotative power (śakyatāvacchedakatva) of that word, while not being an object of the Lord’s will in its capacity as the object of the verbal cognition produced by that word.
It is the state of being the delimitor of the delimitation of the denotability of that word. In reality,
however, those properties which are the delimiters of the objecthood in verbal cognition— those [properties] delimited by each [of them] are the objects of the cognition produced by that word.

In the Lord’s intention in the form "let them be," the property of being the delimitor of the objectness of the cognition [of the word *bhavat*] does not itself become an object of the cognition produced by that word; rather, it functions as a qualifier (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*). Although the property of being the delimitor of the objectness of the cognition...

Although the nature of being an object (*viṣayatā*) is indeed distinct according to the distinction of objects, it is nevertheless designated as "one" because it is delimited by a single, recurring property consisting in the nature of being the delimitor of the objecthood of consciousness (*bodha*).
In this very same manner, by substituting "being an object" (*viṣayatva*) for "not being an object" (*aviṣayatva*) and introducing it as a qualifier...
The state of being the delimitor of the delimitor of capability (śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatva) must be defined;

and it should be understood that this is precisely such things as "hairiness" (lomatva) and "tailingness" (lāṅgūlatva). Regarding the phrase "the object of perceptual cognition" (pratyakṣabuddhiviṣaya), the meaning is "delimited by that which is the delimitor of the objecthood (viṣayatā) of such a cognition. And as for "cognition" (buddhi)—

In this way, the cognition of a jar and so forth by means of the jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and other properties is accomplished through words such as "this" (*ayam*) and so on, which refer back to the speaker himself. However, in cases such as "This is a jar," it is precisely the fact of existing at that particular place and time, which serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the object of the speaker's perception; therefore—

There is no impossibility of their co-occurrence in a non-different [referent]. "For this very reason" means: because the capacity of *idam* and *etad* resides in objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the capacity of *adas* resides in objects of remote cognition (*parokṣabuddhi*), for that very reason.
"The state of having different referents" refers to those—namely, *idam*, *etad*, and *adas*.
The meaning of *idam* and *etad* is one and the same. However, the meaning of *adas* is different from that;
the sense is that the meanings of *idam* and *etad* are distinct according to the principle that "that which is the meaning of *adas* is other than [the meaning of] *idam* and *etad*.
The word "thus" (*evam*) means "having distinct meanings. The phrase "of *etad* and *adas* as well" refers to *etad*.
The meaning is "having as its object that which is perceptible. The intention is that this may mean, in general, "having as its object that which is the content of cognition.

He states the opinion of some: "this" (*idam*). The meaning is "belonging to perception," i.e., "become the object of perception. The word "possible" (*śakyam*) is to be supplied; the same applies to what follows.
And [the word] *samīpataravarti* ("situated closer at hand"). By the particle *ca*, there is an attraction (*anukarṣa*) of the term *pratyakṣagata* ("present before the eyes").

The word *rūpa* means "essential nature" (*svarūpa*). The phrase *viprakṛṣṭaṃ tat* ("that which is remote") means "that which is not present before the eyes. In the expression *parokṣe*, the meaning of the locative case is "denotative of. Thus, [it refers to] the pronoun *adas*.
The meaning is that one should understand [the word "what"] as denoting something imperceptible; this is the final conclusion.

[It means] "qualified by being the object of a desire to know. The meaning is that the referent of the word "what" (kiṃśabda) is the object of a desire to know. Such a desire is conveyed by the word "what" itself when it is uttered. And thus:

The meaning is that in cases such as "What is the pot?", the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is that "the pot is the object of my desire to know. Regarding the term "pervasion" (*vyāpakatva*): the ellipsis is to be supplied as "residing in the delimitors of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), as determined by the delimitors of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*)," as in "All pots," and so forth.

It should be understood that the pervasion of "pot-ness" over "color" consists precisely in the possession of a nature that is not a delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the absence residing in the pot. The reading "tvampadasya" is a corruption;
rather, the correct reading is "yuṣmatpadasya. Otherwise, [the rule would fail] in cases such as "yuvām" and so forth.

This is because it would result in the loss of [the word's] expressive power (*śakti*). Furthermore, it should be understood that in its own system, the term "you" (*tvam*) lacks that very [expressive power].

The phrase "Caitra-ness and so forth of the person being addressed" means "Caitra-ness and so forth, which are co-referential with the state of being the person being addressed. This is because a suffix denoting a state (*bhāvapratyaya*) following a *karmadhāraya* compound conveys a property that delimits the meaning of one word as being co-referential with another property that delimits the meaning of the other word.

And being the object of address at that time consists in being the intended object of the speaker's desire, by virtue of being the substratum of the verbal cognition produced by a sentence occurring immediately after a word such as "Caitra" ending in the first case,
which is uttered for the purpose of addressing at that time— as in "O Caitra, let you eat," and so forth.
By the nominative case following words such as "Caitra," it is precisely this state of being addressed that is conveyed as a qualifier of Caitra and so forth; namely,
Caitra-ness and the like, as characterized by coreferentiality with that [nominative].

The meaning is that the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is the word "you" (*yuṣmad*). Similarly, regarding the word "we" (*asmat*), it connects with the previously mentioned term "delimitor of denotability. Regarding "independent" (*svatantra*):
the meaning is such properties as being Caitra and so forth, which reside in the same locus as the agency of being the utterer of an independent [word].

It should be understood that the utterance belongs specifically to the word *asmad* (we/us), which is intended to denote such a meaning. Furthermore, independence in utterance means not being dependent on the utterance by another;
that is to say, it does not merely repeat the utterance of another. "The cognition of the poet" [is not what is meant].

The sense is that although the poet is the agent of the utterance of the word *asmad* (‘we’) situated in the verse, because he is merely repeating an utterance made by another, there is no cognition [of the speaker] for the poet from the word *asmad* as uttered by that other person. And thus, in the phrase "uttered at such-and-such a time," which forms part of the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *yuṣmad* ('you'), the act of utterance (*uccāraṇa*) is also [included].

The object of apprehension must be understood as being independent [of other factors]. Therefore, even though [the person addressed] is the object of desire by virtue of being the locus of the cognition produced by the sentence "O fool, roar, roar for a moment! When you have been killed by me right here," following the vocative singular word "mūḍha" (fool).
It should not be thought that Suratha’s verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arose from the words of the great sage as they were uttered;

for the statement "he divides the word" does not mean that a word is defined by its division, but rather it is the definition of a word itself. Thus, [the claim] that he "divides" what is "potent" (*śakta*) is indeed untenable. Nevertheless...

It should be understood that there is no inconsistency here, because the word *iti* signifies "and so forth," and because it is a rule that the general definition of a word (*pada*) is stated immediately after the analysis of words (*padavibhāga*). Nor can it be argued that even so, only derivative words like *pācaka* (cook) and the like would exist; for such a word is not denotative of any object whatsoever, since it is merely a sentence (*vākya*).
It should not be argued that because a derivative (yaugika) word is not subsumed under the general definition [of a word],

its classification is untenable; for since the suffix following the verbal root *pac* itself constitutes the word "pācaka," and it possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) toward the agent, there is no obstacle to its classification as a word by virtue of being a *pada*.

The state [of the matter]: it is impossible for a single word to possess both a derivative (yaugika) sense in one meaning and a conventional (rūḍha) sense in another, because the word differs according to the difference in its utterance, and this is due to the principle that what is uttered once [has but one meaning].

With this intention, he explains that "in some cases" (kvacit) means "in a certain sense" (kiñcid-artha), stating: "as for 'in some cases'... As for the objection raised in the root-text: "But surely..."
The inclusion of words such as *maṇḍapa* among the "conventional-derivative" (*rūḍha-yaugika*) is untenable.

For, through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "one who drinks the *maṇḍa* [gruel] or protects it is a *maṇḍapa*," it is possible for them to have meanings such as "the agent of drinking *maṇḍa*"; thus, they belong among the derivative-conventional (*yaugika-rūḍha*) terms.

He says "in the case of *maṇḍapa* etc. to show that such inclusion would indeed occur. Having introduced it thus, he explains: "In this way, the word *maṇḍapa* alone denotes a specific type of house, but the word *maṇḍpa* does not. Furthermore, since that [word *maṇḍapa*] is never etymological (*yaugika*), its inclusion among the conventional (*rūḍha*) words is not untenable."
He intends to explain the term *bhāva*. That is not very elegant;
for even a word that is both etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) can exist with distinct meanings based on its etymological and conventional aspects.

Since the secondary member *maṇḍapa* is conventional in the sense of a "particular house," it is possible to include it among conventional words. For this very reason, [it was stated] in the root-text:
That in which only the meaning of the individual parts is understood is defined as *yaugika* (etymological); thus, this is the definition of the etymological word.

That in which [the meaning] is apprehended through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) independently of the powers of the individual parts is defined as *rūḍha* (conventional); thus, this is the definition of the conventional word. Among these, regarding the definition of the etymological word, there is the *yogarūḍha* (etymological-conventional) type.

The particle *eva* is used precisely to exclude the status of being etymological (*yaugikatva*). Nor should it be argued that, even so, a word such as *udbhid*, which is both etymological and conventional (*yaugika-rūḍha*), would possess etymological meaning in its sense of "that which performs the act of splitting" (*udbhedana-kartṛ*) and so forth; for this is accepted [as a valid case]. This is because, even in the definition of the conventional (*rūḍha*), there is the category of the etymological-conventional (*yogarūḍhi*).
The phrase ending with "nirapekṣayā" (independently) is intended precisely to exclude conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).

Even for the word *udbhid*, which possesses both etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meanings, its conventional status regarding the specific sacrifice as its referent is indeed accepted.
The meaning of "is grasped" (*gṛhyate*) is "is understood. And thus, [this applies] to the secondary member (*upapada*) *maṇḍapa*.

It should not be thought that because [the word *gṛha*] can be established as a conventional term (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "house," its inclusion among conventional terms is untenable. Nor is it the case that the phrase "where" (*yatra*) means "that which is delimited by such-and-such a sequence of phonemes" (*yādṛśānupūrvyavacchinna*), for in the case of a word that is both etymological and conventional (*yaugika-rūḍha*), it is precisely that which is delimited by a single sequence of phonemes that, in a particular context, [conveys] only the meaning of its constituent parts.

It should not be argued that there is no impossibility of conventional usage (*rūḍhatva*) in that case because it conveys only the collective meaning; for that would involve excessive complexity (*prayāsagaurava*). Moreover, since there is no harm in accepting that a term which is both etymological (*yaugika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) may function as either etymological or conventional, this applies even to those [terms] distinct from the etymological-conventional.
There is no contradiction in the classification [of words] because both purely etymological (*yaugika*) and purely conventional (*kevalarūḍha*) types exist;
for it is possible that on the eleventh day after birth, a father might have assigned a name such as "cook" (*pācaka*) through convention, and thus even those names would not be purely etymological.

It should be understood that [the term] "devoid of etymological power" (avayavaśaktirahitayā) must be disregarded, because it would result in the futility of pursuing the analysis as far as "independent of etymological power" (avayavaśaktinirapekṣayā). In reality, since the reading "maṇḍapaḥ vāstu-jale gṛhe" is observed in the Southern *Amarakośa* and other texts, [the word] "japā" found in the Gauḍa version [is an error].

It should be understood that the author used the word *maṇḍapa* because he found the term *maṇḍapa* in many copies of the *Muktāvalī*, following the tradition of Gauḍa manuscripts, where the word *maṇḍapa* is indeed employed in place of *jagatīvan*.

"In the root, it has as its object the power of the individual parts" means that the verbal cognition produced by the knowledge of the power of the individual parts [has that as its object]. "The collective power also exists" means that it also has as its object the meaning recalled by the collective power. According to the literal reading:
Otherwise, even words such as *pācaka* (cook) would result in being both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*), because the word *pācaka*—
which is applied to one who performs cooking and has been conventionally designated by a father on the eleventh day [after birth]—

would possess a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) regarding the referent of its constituent parts' powers. For us, however, [the cognition of] lotus-hood (*padmatva*) arises from the word *paṅkaja* itself with respect to that which is delimited by lotus-hood.

It should be understood that this is because one accepts an beginningless intention (*anādi-tātparya*) regarding the cognition of non-difference in the case of [the compound] *paṅkaja-nikara* (a cluster of mud-born things) and so forth;

whereas, since the verbal cognition "the cook (*pācaka*) is non-different from the agent of cooking (*pāka-kartṛ*)" does not arise, there is no risk of that [term *pācaka*] falling into the category of being merely etymological (*yogarūḍha*). In the root text, the word "it would be" (*syāt*) refers to [the presence of the term] even in the case of the *kumuda* (water-lily).

The point is that since the mere meaning of the individual components is not sublated, it is possible to employ the word *paṅkaja* even in that case, out of a desire for a cognition whose object is that [component] meaning. The term "mere" (*kevala*) means "not having as its object the meaning evoked by the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*). This refers to the knowledge of the etymological meaning.

The meaning is "the knowledge of the meaning of the individual parts. As for the passage beginning with "And not," etc., this objection arises only at first glance; it should be noted by the wise that it does not arise when one attends to the word *kevala* as stated in the root text. Regarding the phrase "because of being an obstacle": [this refers to] the state of being an obstacle (*pratibandhakatva*).

The phrase "of a cognition whose object is not contradictory," and so forth, is used. Therefore, it should be noted that even though a certainty of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*)—which is not itself contradictory to the *parāmarśa* (the inferential consideration)—acts as an obstacle to inference, this does not result in a violation of the stated rule. Regarding the phrase "due to proximity (*sānnidhya*), etc.": [an objection is raised]—"But in the root text, [is it not the case that] the lotus-ness (*padmatva*)-delimited..."

The moderns have stated that, because the meaning of the constituent parts— the agent of the act of joining— is present as a proximate object of cognition, there occurs only a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*) therein; thus, the aforementioned relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) is not supported by valid authority.

That is not tenable; for even when intending *kumuda* (the white water-lily), the use of the word *paṅkaja* is accepted through the etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*), and thus it would follow that there too the cognition "a lotus non-different from the agent of arising in mud" would arise. Nor is that the case there...

It should not be argued that this undesirable consequence does not arise simply because there is no presentation (*upasthiti*) of that which is delimited by the property of being a lotus (*padmatva*).
To dispel the doubt that— since the word *paṅkaja* possesses a conventional power (*smāraka-śakti*) directed toward a lotus, the recollection of a lotus from it is necessary—
the phrase "by proximity" (*sānnidhyāt*) indicates that in that context, the word *paṅkaja* [functions] with respect to the object in the form of a lotus.
He states that it was said precisely because of the existence of *tātparya* (intentional meaning): "of words denoting individuals.

This means words that denote individuals such as jars, cloths, and so forth. The inclusion of the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding words whose primary referent is a universal (*jāti*). [The phrase] "referring to what is proximate" (*sannihitaparatva*)...

The meaning is that [the word] has as its intended referent (*tātparya*) an individual (*vyakti*) that is presented without mediation. For this very reason, when it is said "bring the jar," if a jar is present nearby, people do not proceed to bring a jar located at a distance; such is the sense.
